World.title: What Ancient Kazakh Traditions Can Teach Us About Surviving Extreme Heat
World.content:
ASTANA – As climate change fuels increasingly intense heat waves, staying safe in extreme temperatures has become a growing concern across Kazakhstan. This summer, temperatures have climbed above 40 degrees Celsius in several regions, testing both people’s endurance and public health systems.

While modern households rely on air conditioners and fans, Kazakhstan’s nomadic ancestors developed practical ways to stay cool long before electricity. According to a candidate of historical sciences Saltanat Asanova, many of these centuries-old practices remain relevant today.

“Traditional culture, livelihoods and daily life were always closely connected to the natural environment and its changes. People were prepared for both cold and heat,” Asanova told The Astana Times.

For nomadic herders, extreme summer heat was rarely a major problem because they moved with the seasons.

“Nomads who migrated year-round spent summers in cooler areas, either farther north or in high mountain pastures. Moving livestock to alpine grazing lands was the primary way to escape the summer heat. Even on the hottest days, temperatures in the mountains remain significantly lower than in the steppe,” Asanova said.

Daily routines also followed the rhythm of the sun. Work began at dawn, paused during the hottest midday hours and resumed in the evening as temperatures dropped.

“Most household and pastoral work was completed after sunset, when the heat subsided,” she said.

The science behind a cooler yurt

The yurt, the traditional portable dwelling of Kazakh nomads, played a crucial role in keeping families cool.

According to Asanova, the yurt’s design created constant natural airflow. The shanyrak, the circular opening at the top of the roof, was left open during the day, allowing hot air to rise and escape while cooler air remained inside.

To maximize ventilation, yurts were carefully positioned according to prevailing winds. Although entrances traditionally faced southeast, their orientation could be adjusted depending on local wind conditions. Lifting the edges of the felt covering allowed air to circulate freely through the structure.

“When temperatures became especially high, the side felt coverings were removed entirely, leaving only the wooden lattice frame and reed mats. The small gaps between the reeds created excellent ventilation, helping maintain a comfortable indoor temperature without any additional cooling devices,” Asanova said.

Historical accounts by travelers who visited the Kazakh steppe during the summer describe yurts as being noticeably cooler than the outside air.

The felt roof continued to protect residents from direct sunlight.

“Felt has unique insulating properties. It retains warmth in winter while preventing solar heat from penetrating the dwelling during summer,” Asanova said.

Dressing for the heat

Despite the high temperatures, Kazakhs traditionally wore long, loose-fitting clothing rather than exposing their skin.

“It may seem paradoxical, but the hotter it became, the more layers people wore. Quilted robes provided better protection from the sun than lightweight clothing or bare skin. Like felt, multiple layers acted as insulation against overheating,” Asanova said.

She noted that headwear was equally essential.

“Felt hats effectively protected the head from the scorching sun while preventing excessive heat exposure,” she said.

Summer diet

Seasonal eating also helped people cope with the heat.

“During summer, meat was consumed only rarely. The diet consisted primarily of dairy products such as kymyz, airan, shubat, and milk-based kozhe, a traditional grain-and-milk soup,” Asanova said.

Drinks were stored in leather containers known as burdyuks, whose natural materials allowed air circulation while keeping liquids cool. Wooden tubs and clay vessels were also commonly used.

“Natural materials help maintain a relatively stable temperature regardless of the weather. For the same reason, water was traditionally stored in clay containers or leather bags,” she said.

Asanova noted that although tea remained an expensive imported commodity, both nomadic and settled communities embraced an unusual practice: drinking hot tea during hot weather.

“They followed one principle: the hotter the weather, the hotter the drink. People avoided cold water because they believed it disrupted the body’s natural heat regulation and made the heat feel even more intense. Instead, they drank hot green tea, which helps the body adapt to high temperatures and promotes natural cooling,” she said.

Modern medical advice

As heat waves become more frequent across Kazakhstan, general practitioner Malika Muratbekova said traditional advice on coping with extreme temperatures remains relevant, including avoiding excessive consumption of ice-cold water, especially during meals.

“Very cold liquids can slow digestion. The body has to expend extra energy warming the stomach, which can leave a person feeling even more fatigued,” Muratbekova said in an interview with The Astana Times.

She recommends drinking water in small amounts throughout the day, avoiding sugary soft drinks, and wearing loose-fitting, light-colored clothing made from natural or cooling fabrics with ultraviolet protection.

Muratbekova also advised protecting the head with a hat and cooling the body gradually.

“You can place a cooling towel or damp cloth around your neck. Portable fans are also becoming increasingly common. Taking a cool shower, using a spray bottle or damp cloth to moisten the skin can help lower body temperature. However, avoid ice-cold showers because a sudden drop in temperature can place unnecessary stress on the body,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Completes Key Stage of Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has completed the most technically challenging stage of the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable project after an undersea cable reached the country’s Caspian coast on Aug. 5, marking a milestone in efforts to establish a new high-speed digital corridor linking Asia and Europe.

The submarine cable, laid along the Caspian Sea floor between Aktau and Sumgait, will directly connect the digital infrastructure of Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, providing an alternative international data transmission route designed to improve connectivity, strengthen network resilience and expand the two countries’ role in Eurasian digital transit.

The project is being implemented by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom International, while the joint venture CaspiLink B.V. will oversee both construction and future operation of the network.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhtelecom Chairman Bagdat Mussin and AzerTelecom International Chief Executive Ana Nakashidze inspected the completion of the marine installation phase aboard the cable-laying vessel.

“We have completed the most difficult stage of the Trans-Caspian Fiber Optic Cable project – laying the cable along the Caspian Sea floor. The new route will strengthen Kazakhstan’s digital connectivity with global data networks and create the foundation for the further development of artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and modern data centers,” Madiyev said.

According to the ministry, the government completed the regulatory, customs and organizational procedures required to begin construction without administrative delays.

The project began in 2025 with engineering surveys, route selection and factory testing of a specially armored submarine cable manufactured in China. Engineers designed the route to avoid anchorage zones and military training areas while securing the necessary environmental approvals in Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region.

Construction at sea began in July 2026 using a specialized cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons. Around 70 specialists participated in the round-the-clock operation.

The cable had previously been transported from China to the port of Kuryk before being shipped to Baku, where it was transferred to the cable-laying vessel for installation across the Caspian Sea.

Work is now focused on connecting the cable to coastal infrastructure. Ground infrastructure, commissioning and system testing are expected to be completed this autumn. Unlike many strategic infrastructure projects, the Trans-Caspian cable is being financed entirely by the participating telecommunications operators without state budget funding.

Part of a broader digital corridor

The project forms part of Kazakhstan’s broader strategy to position itself as a regional digital hub alongside its expanding transport and logistics ambitions.

For years, Kazakhstan has sought to strengthen the Middle Corridor connecting China and Europe through the Caspian Sea. While much of that effort has focused on railways, ports and highways, officials increasingly argue that digital infrastructure will become equally important for regional connectivity.

The new fiber-optic route is expected to provide lower-latency and more resilient international data transmission while reducing dependence on existing communication routes. It also complements Kazakhstan’s wider digital agenda, which includes investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure, cloud computing and data centers intended to serve regional markets.

By creating an additional high-capacity data corridor across the Caspian, the project illustrates how Kazakhstan’s concept of connectivity is expanding beyond physical trade routes to include digital infrastructure.

World.title: Kazakhstan Moves to Build Nationwide Flood and Drought Early Warning System
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan signed an agreement on Aug. 4 to develop a nationwide flood and drought early warning system, signaling a broader shift from responding to water emergencies toward anticipating them. The project, developed jointly by the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation’s Information and Analytical Center and Agip Karachaganak, will integrate data on the country’s water infrastructure into a unified forecasting system.

The agreement was signed during the third meeting of the Development Partners Coordination Council under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, which brought together government agencies, international organizations, financial institutions, development partners, diplomats and private-sector representatives to review progress on Kazakhstan’s Water Partnership Initiative 2024–2030.

The early warning system is expected to combine hydrological data with information on water infrastructure to improve monitoring of flood and drought risks nationwide. Rather than focusing solely on responding to emergencies after they occur, the initiative aims to strengthen preparedness by providing authorities with better forecasting and decision-making tools.

The project reflects a broader evolution in Kazakhstan’s water policy as the country faces increasing pressure from climate variability, recurring droughts and floods, growing demand for water resources and the need to modernize aging infrastructure.

Alongside the forecasting initiative, the ministry signed additional agreements to establish AquaLab, a national center for water innovation, STEM education and environmental awareness. The Water Resources Information and Analytical Center signed cooperation agreements with the Caravan of Knowledge Corporate Foundation, while a separate trilateral agreement involving the Association of Environmental Organizations of Kazakhstan and the Central Asia and Caucasus representative office of The Coca-Cola Company will finance and implement the project.

According to Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov, water conservation has become a new model for managing Kazakhstan’s water resources rather than a standalone policy direction.

“Water conservation is no longer a separate area of work but a new model of water resources management,” he said.

According to him, infrastructure solutions must be accompanied by modern management technologies. Digital tools should create a unified information space, while the introduction of new technologies must be supported by specialist training and the development of a culture of responsible water use.

The initiatives were presented within the framework of the Development Partners Coordination Council, established jointly by the ministry and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Kazakhstan in September 2024. The platform now brings together more than 40 international partners working on water-sector development.

UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan Katarzyna Wawiernia said the council has evolved beyond a forum for discussion into a mechanism that translates cooperation into concrete projects.

“The real value of this work is measured not by the number of meetings but by the joint solutions that are already being transformed into investment projects and improvements in public policy,” she said.

Taken together, the agreements suggest Kazakhstan’s water reforms are entering a new phase. While investment in reservoirs, canals and irrigation systems remains essential, policymakers are increasingly pairing physical infrastructure with digital technologies, forecasting capabilities and research. By integrating data, innovation and international partnerships into a single strategy, Kazakhstan is seeking to build a water management system that is better equipped to anticipate future risks.

World.title: Kazakhstan Leads Central Asia in 2026 Legatum Prosperity Index
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked first among Central Asian countries in the 2026 Legatum Prosperity Index, placing 66th out of 161 economies worldwide, according to the latest report published by the Prosperity Institute.

The annual index assesses countries across more than 130 indicators grouped into three broad pillars: prosperity, freedom and society. The 2026 edition introduced an updated methodology that places greater emphasis on balanced performance across all categories, rather than allowing strong results in one area to offset weaknesses in another.

Kazakhstan ranked 52nd globally in the Development pillar, 45th in Society, and 47th in Integrity of Society. The country recorded its strongest results in education, where it placed 32nd worldwide, and in Integrity of Families, ranking 30th. Kazakhstan also placed 53rd globally for living conditions.

Among Central Asian countries, Kazakhstan outperformed the Kyrgyz Republic (87th), Uzbekistan (94th), Tajikistan (129th), and Turkmenistan (150th). It also ranked ahead of Russia, which placed 103rd overall.

The report identifies Switzerland as the world’s most prosperous country in 2026, followed by Norway, Ireland, Denmark and Finland. According to the institute, Switzerland topped the ranking due to consistently strong performance across all major dimensions without significant weaknesses.

The Legatum Prosperity Index is an annual global assessment that measures long-term prosperity by evaluating economic performance alongside institutional quality, governance, education, health, social capital, personal freedom and other factors affecting quality of life.

World.title: Armenia begins shift from Russia towards EU – but finish line remains distant
World.content:
Armenia between Europe and Russia

Against this backdrop, the European Union pledged to “stand by Armenia”. EU leaders have already announced tens of millions of dollars in financial assistance and opened the bloc’s markets to Armenian goods that had suddenly ceased to meet Russian quality standards. More importantly, Brussels has expressed interest in further deepening ties with Yerevan, while Armenia’s re-elected leadership says the election results demonstrate the public’s desire to continue along the country’s European path.

Parliamentary elections in Armenia are over, but the political—and geopolitical—debate continues. Many viewed the vote as a de facto referendum on the country’s future orientation: Russia or the European Union.During the election campaign, Moscow imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian food products, a move widely interpreted in Armenia as an attempt to influence public opinion. Contrary to some expectations, Russia not only kept those trade restrictions in place after the election but tightened them.

JAMnews reviewed the latest developments and spoke to analysts with opposing views. Residents of Armenia also shared their opinions on how they believe the country should shape its future.

Yerevan residents rush to work in the morning. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

How Armenia’s pivot took shape

Few people remember now, but immediately after the 2018 “Velvet Revolution”, led by then-opposition figure and now Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, he insisted that his government would not pursue any geopolitical realignment. At the time, Armenia was already a member of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). Years later, speaking from podiums in both Europe and Yerevan, the same Pashinyan has declared Armenia’s aspiration to join the European Union.

So what happened in between? Over the past several years, the entire security architecture of the South Caucasus has unraveled, triggering a snowball effect. Initially, relations between Yerevan and Moscow developed without major friction. Then came the 2020 Karabakh war. Armenia was defeated and ceased to be the guarantor of Nagorno-Karabakh’s security. Formally, Yerevan had no grounds to hold Moscow responsible in 2020. Nagorno-Karabakh was not part of Armenia, and the agreements signed between the two countries applied only to Armenia itself, not to the unrecognised entity.

However, events then took an unexpected turn.

Over the following two years, Azerbaijan launched several military operations on Armenia’s internationally recognised territory. Yerevan appealed to its allies in the CSTO for assistance, but received neither military support nor even a political assessment of the situation.

The allies responded that it was first necessary to establish where exactly the escalation had taken place, arguing that the Armenia-Azerbaijan border had not been formally delimited. Pashinyan replied sharply:

“To say that there is no border between Armenia and Azerbaijan is to claim that the Collective Security Treaty Organization has no area of responsibility. And if there is no area of responsibility, then there is no organisation.”

Since then, Yerevan, finding itself alone in the face of what it viewed as an external security threat, has frozen its participation in the CSTO and turned increasingly towards Europe. According to some analysts, the price of that shift was Armenia’s official recognition of Nagorno-Karabakh as part of Azerbaijan. In return, the European Union deployed a civilian monitoring mission to Armenia, which helped stabilise the situation along the border with Azerbaijan. Armenia also secured the EU’s political backing.

Retiree Andrey Karapetyan shares his views on European integration. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Shift gathered pace

These developments on the ground were inevitably followed by political change. The entire Armenia-Azerbaijan negotiation process shifted to Western platforms—an outcome few had anticipated. Since the conflict began in the 1990s, Moscow had served as the principal mediator and facilitator of the peace talks.

Following the events of September 2023, when Azerbaijan’s one-day military operation prompted the entire Armenian population to flee Nagorno-Karabakh, Russia effectively lost its influence in the region.

At the same time, Russia also lost its standing among much of Armenia’s population, no longer being viewed as a friendly state.

A park in Yerevan, where locals gather to play backgammon and discuss politics. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Although Russia formally remains Armenia’s strategic ally, many Armenians have not forgotten that Russian peacekeepers effectively acted as bystanders, failing to fulfil their mission of protecting the Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh. Following the CSTO’s refusal to defend Armenia’s territorial integrity, relations between Moscow and Yerevan cooled even further. The Armenian leadership also adopted a more outspoken tone towards Russia, both in its rhetoric and in its actions.

At the same time, contacts between the Armenian government and its European partners intensified. Brussels allocated hundreds of millions of dollars to support political and economic reforms in Armenia, as well as strengthen the country’s borders. France also began supplying Armenia with military equipment. The culmination of these developments came on 17 October 2023, when speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared:

“The Republic of Armenia is ready to be as close to the European Union as the European Union considers possible. Our joint statement with President von der Leyen says: ‘In these difficult times, the EU and Armenia stand shoulder to shoulder.'”

In the years that followed, Pashinyan repeatedly stated that Armenia would seek EU membership. The parliamentary elections held in June and their outcome only reinforced the government’s determination.

“Last year, we adopted a law launching the process of accession to the European Union, which, I would remind you, was initiated by civil society. I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: August, 2008. Chronology of the war over South Ossetia in facts and photos
World.content:
August five-day war: what happened

On August 8 2008, Georgian and Russian forces fought in South Ossetia in a conflict that would last five days and come to be known as the Five Day War.

JAMnews has published a detailed, chronological review of how the war started and unfolded over those five days.
