World.title: ‘There are signs Armenia is heading for ‘divorce’ from the Russian-led EAEU,’ says Armenian political analyst
World.content:
Possible developments in Armenia-EAEU relations

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has travelled to Kyrgyzstan for a two-day working visit to attend a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council. The agenda includes economic cooperation, trade, transport, customs regulation and integration within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

Pashinyan’s visit comes amid Russian restrictions on Armenian goods and growing tensions between the two countries.

Before the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council convened, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk said trade between Armenia and Russia had fallen by two-thirds. He described the decline as “dramatic”.

Armenia’s prime minister has urged people to see the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify the country’s economy.

At the same time, Armenian analysts say there are signs of a “divorce” from the EAEU. Some believe Yerevan may now decide to make a sharp and irreversible break.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk said:

“We expected the situation now unfolding between the EAEU and Armenia. Over the past three to four years, we repeatedly warned our Armenian colleagues about these risks, including the risk of a decline in trade.

“In 2024, trade between Russia and Armenia reached a record high of around $12bn. That was a huge figure. Last year, it fell to about $8bn.

“This year, however, trade has dropped dramatically. It is down by around two-thirds compared with 2025. The current trend suggests it will continue to decline.”

Pashinyan: “The EAEU is de facto paralysed”

The Armenian prime minister says Russian restrictions on Armenian goods are not only Armenia’s problem but also a problem for the EAEU itself.

“In effect, the Eurasian Economic Union is paralysed and no longer functioning. If this issue is not resolved quickly, let me predict that it will mark the beginning of the end for the EAEU,” Nikol Pashinyan said recently.

Russia leads the Eurasian Economic Union. Armenia has been a full member of the bloc since 2015. Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are also members.

Pashinyan also said the EAEU was facing a deepening crisis.

“If this issue is not resolved quickly, I am 100% certain that Armenia will overcome this problem, not the EAEU,” he said.

He added that he intended to raise and discuss all outstanding issues within the EAEU itself.

Comment

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan says:

“If Russia’s pressure on Armenia before the elections was mainly aimed at supporting pro-Russian political forces, its increased pressure now is directed primarily at Armenia’s foreign policy and its efforts to diversify its international partnerships.

“Pashinyan openly hinted at this when he said Armenia could not give up its right to have alternatives. The prime minister also warned that continued economic pressure from Russia could trigger the ‘collapse of the EAEU’. Armenia sees the greatest problems within this multilateral framework and is responding through the same framework.

“On 30 July, for example, Armenia banned imports of tomato paste for six months not only from Russia but also from other EAEU member states. This was clearly a signal to its partners that they should not treat Armenia unfairly.

“The situation closely resembles the events of autumn 2022. Azerbaijan attacked Armenia’s sovereign territory and later occupied parts of it. Armenia then called on the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) to fulfil its obligations under the alliance’s rules, but the bloc refused. That refusal ultimately led Armenia to effectively leave the CSTO.

“Four years later, Armenia has virtually no ties with the CSTO. It no longer takes part in the bloc’s activities, funding or meetings. The relationship can be described as a ‘de facto divorce’ between Armenia and the CSTO.

“The situation is harder to imagine in the case of the EAEU because the bloc is far more integrated. It has a common customs regime, a shared pool of financial transfers, and over the past decade Armenia’s economy has adapted to the logic of the EAEU.

“That means a split between Armenia and the EAEU could happen suddenly and completely.

“The first signs of the mutual disappointment that usually precedes a ‘divorce’ are already clear.”

Context

Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian fruit and vegetables ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary elections. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products, citing quality concerns.

Armenian officials and analysts, however, viewed the measures through the prism of the election campaign. Most analysts expected Russia to ease the pressure after the vote. Instead, Moscow not only kept the restrictions in place but introduced new ones.

In response, the Armenian government launched support programmes for businesses. Exporters began redirecting shipments to the Middle East and the European Union. The EU is also expected to approve a scheme granting autonomous trade measures for Armenian products. The plan would provide significant trade preferences for Armenian exports. Armenia would become the first country without EU candidate status or a free trade agreement with the bloc to benefit from the mechanism.

At the same time, Moscow has urged Armenia to decide quickly whether it wants to move towards the EU or remain in the EAEU. It has also called for a referendum on the issue.

Yerevan says there are currently no grounds for holding such a referendum. Armenian officials argue that the country should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, formally place the issue on the political agenda.

The issue of a referendum also came up during a phone call between Pashinyan and Putin on 27 July, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

However, the Kremlin’s readout of the conversation omitted Pashinyan’s response that it was too early to hold a referendum. It also made no mention of the prime minister raising Russia’s restrictions on Armenian imports. Pashinyan later said the measures “contradict the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and the regulations of the Eurasian Economic Union”. He called for urgent steps to resolve the issue.

Possible developments in Armenia-EAEU relations

World.title: Attack on Georgian comedian accompanied by coordinated information campaign
World.content:
A smear campaign against Georgian comedian Onise Okriashvili involving pro-government media, politicians and coordinated online accounts began before he was attacked, before shifting afterwards to justify the violence and express support for the alleged attacker.

That is the main finding of a study by the Myth Detector project, which says the campaign unfolded systematically across multiple channels, including media outlets and social media.

On 23 July 2026, three men ambushed and brutally assaulted pro-European protest participant, comedian and stand-up performer Onise Okriashvili in Tbilisi over a joke he made about renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze. The suspects were arrested but later released on bail. One of their friends, professional wrestler Giorgi Kartvelishvili, subsequently announced the creation of the “People’s Movement” together with like-minded supporters, saying its aim was to “protect Georgian values, ideals and traditions.”

According to the Myth Detector study, pro-government media outlets and Facebook pages began circulating old videos and public statements by Onise Okriashvili several days before the attack. The material was taken out of context and presented in a way that portrayed the comedian as someone who insulted Georgia’s national, cultural and religious values.

The study says that after the attack, social media and pro-government media promoted narratives claiming the assault had been triggered by Okriashvili’s joke about Nodar Dumbadze. It found that posts and graphics shared from 24 July onwards sought to downplay the attackers’ responsibility and portray them as “defenders of the nation’s honour”.

Identical graphics were circulated simultaneously by supporters of the ruling Georgian Dream party, anti-opposition Facebook pages and pro-government commentators. The central message was that the main suspect, Nikoloz Khurtsilava, did not deserve punishment because he had “defended the national honour of Georgians.”

According to the study, these narratives were also echoed by members of the ruling party. Georgian President Mikheil Kavelashvili focused not on the assault itself but on the inadmissibility of insulting Nodar Dumbadze. MP Dimitri Samkharadze said he was prepared to act as a guarantor for the defendant, while another lawmaker, Irakli Zarkua, condemned the violence but added that public outrage over jokes targeting the church, the patriarch and prominent writers had been predictable. Levan Kochloshvili, a representative of the pro-government People’s Power party, said he disagreed with the moral condemnation of the accused.

The Myth Detector study also says the campaign to discredit Okriashvili continued after the attack using new material. Pro-government platforms again circulated old videos of the comedian, including clips related to religious issues, as well as a previously shared video in which they claimed he mocked elderly women selling sunflower seeds. According to the study’s authors, this shifted attention away from the assault itself and onto the victim’s remarks.

The report also highlights signs of coordinated online activity. Researchers identified fake accounts that expressed support for both the man accused of carrying out the attack and the movement later announced by Giorgi Kartvelishvili. Some of the accounts posted identical comments, complete with the same grammatical mistakes, beneath stories published by pro-government media, while others used other people’s names and photographs to conceal their identities.

One of the study’s main findings concerns a case in which pro-government media presented a Facebook post by a previously identified troll as the opinion of a real person. According to the authors, the post, which attacked Onise Okriashvili and defended the alleged attacker, was then simultaneously amplified by 13 pro-government online outlets and the Facebook pages of two television channels.

Myth Detector also says part of the campaign relied on paid promotion through sponsored posts. These portrayed Okriashvili and his supporters as “anti-Georgian forces”, while the alleged attacker’s statements were promoted in a way that justified the violence.

Attack on comedian in Georgia

World.title: Returning Abkhaz citizenship to ethnic Georgians: integration or a security threat?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s parliament is set to consider restoring Abkhaz nationality status to residents of the Gali district. The opposition is firmly against the move, arguing that it would pose a threat to national security.

The parliamentary committee on state and legal policy has approved amendments to the law on civil status acts that would extend the right to restore Abkhaz nationality status and surnames to foreign nationals permanently residing in Abkhazia who are ethnic Abkhazians, as well as “direct descendants of people who lost their Abkhaz nationality as a result of anti-Abkhaz national policies pursued in the 19th and 20th centuries.”

Behind this lengthy wording lies one specific group: ethnic Georgians living in Abkhazia’s Gali district. In 2011, the overwhelming majority of them – around 30,000 people – were stripped of their Abkhaz citizenship on the grounds that they also held Georgian citizenship.

In place of Abkhaz passports, they were issued permanent residence permits allowing them to live indefinitely in the breakaway republic.

Calls to allow residents of the Gali district to regain Abkhaz citizenship have periodically resurfaced in debates over the full integration of the area’s population.

One proposal has been to allow them to change their recorded ethnicity in official documents from Georgian to Abkhaz. Supporters argue there is a historical basis for this, as some Gali residents have surnames of Abkhaz origin, and their ancestors are believed to have been assimilated into the Georgian population at the turn of the 20th century.

Under Abkhazia’s current citizenship law, such a change in official records would automatically entitle Gali residents to regain Abkhaz citizenship, even if they also hold Georgian citizenship.

The proposed amendments to the law on civil status acts are due to be debated at the next parliamentary session, and judging by the opposition’s reaction, the discussion is likely to be heated.

“Pushing this bill through under the current foreign policy circumstances creates additional and extremely dangerous risks that could be exploited by external forces to undermine stability and national security,” five opposition groups said in a joint statement.

They argue that if Gali residents regain Abkhaz passports while retaining Georgian citizenship, they could play a much greater role in the republic’s political life by running for parliament or the presidency, initiating referendums and influencing key political decisions.

According to the opposition, “such a prospect poses a direct threat to the national interests and fundamental rights of the Abkhaz people, secured at the cost of enormous sacrifice.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhaz citizenship for ethnic Georgians

World.title: Head of US-based TRIPP+ foundation holds talks in Armenia: Key takeaways
World.content:
TRIPP+ Foundation chief visits Yerevan

Konstantin Sokolov, head of the TRIPP+ foundation, is visiting Armenia. Armenia’s Foreign Ministry disclosed the visit in a statement identifying Sokolov as president of the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Foundation.

The ministry said Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan met Aryeh Lightstone, senior adviser to the US special envoy for peace missions. Konstantin Sokolov also attended the meeting.

“The participants discussed ongoing efforts to implement the TRIPP programme. Both sides emphasised their commitment to launching the programme on the ground as quickly as possible.”

A day earlier, reports said the US authorities had doubled funding for TRIPP+, increasing it from an initial $201m to $402m.

The TRIPP+ Foundation was established as a separate investment fund. Its primary role is to finance the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project. The project centres on a road linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The Armenian government views the route as part of its Crossroads of Peace initiative to reopen regional transport links. According to a US State Department representative, TRIPP+ has the authority to provide loans, make equity investments and award grants to support strategic private-sector development. Delaware’s official corporate registry also lists the organisation under the name Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund. Fifty-two-year-old financier and investor Konstantin Sokolov also heads Dynamic Frontier Holdings. The company recently acquired Armenia’s Teghut copper and molybdenum mine. Since 2024, Sokolov has also owned a 20% stake in Armenian mobile operator Viva Armenia. Sokolov was born in Russia and moved to the United States at the age of 21. He is known for investments in telecommunications, energy and financial services. He owns the Chicago-based investment firm IJS Investments and Zurich-based Gotthard Investment AG, which focuses on financial services, energy and real estate. He is also involved in the Northern Pillar Energy consortium, which develops clean energy projects and fibre-optic cable infrastructure linking Africa and Europe.

Details of the Foreign Ministry talks

According to Armenia’s Foreign Ministry, the participants held detailed discussions on advancing regional connectivity and making the most of the region’s competitive advantages.

“The participants exchanged views on how Armenia could integrate most effectively into the international transport and infrastructure network.”

The participants also discussed opportunities to expand trade and economic cooperation and strengthen Armenia’s economic and energy resilience.

“The participants welcomed the recent increase in high-level visits and the agreements reached between the two countries. They also highlighted the tangible progress in developing the Armenia–US Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which has resulted in part from the implementation of the three memorandums signed in Washington on 8 August last year. Among the key initiatives, they singled out rapidly expanding cooperation in artificial intelligence and the launch of the data processing centre (AI factory) being built as the first phase of Firebird AI’s flagship project,” the ministry said.

The participants also discussed the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process, focusing on how it could unlock the region’s development potential.

TRIPP+ funding earmarked for projects in Armenia

According to the official US government spending database, USAspending.gov, the US State Department has doubled funding for the TRIPP+ Foundation. The database identifies Armenia as the programme’s primary geographic focus, reflecting the fact that the funding supports implementation of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project, which will run through Armenian territory.

The database also specifies that the project aims to establish a transport route “through southern Armenia to connect the South Caucasus with the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor.”

The first tranche of $201m was originally scheduled to run until 31 December 2036. On 16 July, the US State Department doubled the funding, while leaving the implementation deadline unchanged.

“The increase in US funding comes as Washington seeks to expand its involvement in developing transport and economic connectivity in the South Caucasus and to advance projects linking the region with the Trans-Caspian Corridor.”

The TRIPP project is expected to influence not only regional trade and logistics but also the broader strategic landscape of the South Caucasus.

Context: the link between TRIPP and TRIPP+

The leaders of Armenia, the United States and Azerbaijan signed a joint declaration establishing the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) at the Washington summit on 8 August 2025.

On 26 May 2026, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio initialled a framework agreement on strategic cooperation for the TRIPP project in Yerevan. The two sides formally signed the agreement remotely a few days later.

Armenia has already launched the ratification process. The government approved the draft agreement on 16 July. The Constitutional Court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s Constitution. The two sides must also finalise two additional documents:

a shareholders’ agreement;

the charter of the joint Armenian-US company, TRIPP Development Company.

During the project’s initial phase, the United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years after the initial 49-year term, Armenia’s share will increase to 49%.

The TRIPP Development Company will oversee the project’s design and implementation. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said TRIPP+ would have an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company, which Armenia will establish. The United States created the TRIPP+ company under TRIPP Development Company-USA, and it will take responsibility for attracting investment to finance the programme.

TRIPP+ Foundation chief visits Yerevan

World.title: Why Georgia’s prime minister is talking about ‘Russophobia’ ahead of anniversary of August war
World.content:
Just days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement on what he described as “Russophobia”.

In the statement, Kobakhidze draws connections between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic politics and the rhetoric of the Georgian opposition. He argues that the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine to “fuel Russophobia among its agents worldwide, including in Georgia.”

The prime minister accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current hardline stance as “Russophobia”.

The statement has reignited debate over the 2008 war. This time, however, the focus extends beyond how the war began and Russia’s responsibility for it. Instead, the prime minister shifts attention away from Russia’s actions and towards the position of his political opponents in Georgia.

The opposition has questioned not only the substance of Kobakhidze’s remarks, but also the timing of their publication. Why did the prime minister choose to speak about “Russophobia” on the eve of the war’s anniversary? Why does his statement focus on anything other than Russia’s responsibility? And what is the government doing to address the continuing occupation and the possibility of further annexation?

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

One of the central arguments in Kobakhidze’s statement is that Georgia’s opposition groups did not adopt a hardline stance towards Russia after the 2008 war. According to the prime minister, their position changed only in 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Kobakhidze notes that after the August 2008 war, Mikheil Saakashvili’s government chose to maintain economic, tourism and cultural ties with Russia. He also points out that the government unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

“After Russia occupied parts of Georgia in 2008 and recognised the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the United National Movement not only refrained from pursuing a hardline policy towards Russia, but shortly after the war its leader personally welcomed Russian citizens at the border and encouraged them to visit Georgia as tourists and invest in the country.”

According to Kobakhidze, neither members of the then government nor figures who are now in opposition objected to that policy. He specifically named opposition politicians Elene Khoshtaria, Zurab Japaridze and Misha Mshvildadze.

“We all remember how today’s leading ‘Russophobes’ — Elene Khoshtaria, Zurab Japaridze, Misha Mshvildadze and others — welcomed Russian tourists, Russian money, which apparently ‘didn’t smell’ at the time, and closer trade, economic and cultural ties with Russia.”

Based on this, Kobakhidze argues that the opposition’s current anti-Russian rhetoric and what he calls “Russophobia” are not the result of a consistent political position but of instructions received from abroad. In his statement, he describes his opponents as “foreign agents” and links their actions to the “deep state” and the “Global War Party.”

“The foreign agents declared Russia their sworn enemy only after it launched its second invasion of Ukraine.”

Kobakhidze asks why the same attitude did not emerge in 2008, when Georgia itself became the victim of Russian aggression.

“A logical question arises: why did they become Russophobes now, rather than when Georgia was under attack? Do they not even formally regard Georgia as their homeland? Is Ukraine their homeland instead?”

Another of his arguments concerns Elene Khoshtaria, who receives inherited royalties from Russia for the work of her late father, Soviet-era theatre director Goga Khoshtaria. Kobakhidze presents this as an example of what he describes as the opposition’s inconsistency.

“We all know that Russophobic politicians, NGO representatives, journalists and activists have remained silent about the millions of Russian roubles transferred to Elene Khoshtaria from the Russian state budget.”

Timing of the statement

Kobakhidze published his statement just a few days before the 18th anniversary of the August 2008 war.

At this time of year, Georgians traditionally commemorate those killed in the conflict, internally displaced people and the territories occupied by Russia. Critics have therefore questioned why the prime minister shifted the focus away from Russia’s responsibility and towards what he describes as the opposition’s “Russophobia”.

Irakli Pavlenishvili of the United National Movement views the statement in that context. In his opinion, raising the issue of “Russophobia” in an occupied country on the eve of the war’s anniversary is no coincidence.

“Promoting this narrative just before the anniversary of the August war is exactly what the Kremlin would want and encourage. It is impossible to believe that complaining about Russophobia in occupied Georgia at such a moment is a coincidence.”

Pavlenishvili argues that this rhetoric pushes Russia’s responsibility into the background while turning Georgia’s former government and the opposition into the main targets of political debate.

“This is another deliberate psychological and propaganda operation against the Georgian people. But they will have to accept that they will not be able to weaken or destroy anti-occupation sentiment among the Georgian public.”

Grigol Gegelia of the Lelo – Strong Georgia movement also emphasised the timing of the statement. He argues that, in the days leading up to the anniversary of the August war, Kobakhidze chose to confront fellow Georgian citizens instead of Russia.

According to Gegelia, the prime minister’s main focus at this time should have been Russia’s aggression and Georgia’s security.

“First and foremost, he should have been talking about Russian aggression and about the fact that Georgia was the first link in the chain of events that later continued elsewhere.”

What do Kobakhidze’s critics say?

Kobakhidze’s critics do not deny that Saakashvili’s government welcomed Russian tourists and maintained some economic ties with Russia after the war. The disagreement lies in how that policy should be interpreted.

Opposition figures distinguish between the Russian government and ordinary Russian citizens. In their view, welcoming tourists did not amount to supporting the Kremlin’s policies.

Gigi Tsereteli, leader of the European Georgia party, says the government sought to avoid creating the image of a xenophobic state. At the same time, he notes, Tbilisi continued to demand that Russia comply with the 12 August 2008 ceasefire agreement.

“Georgia was not a xenophobic country. The idea was to show that many Russians themselves opposed Putin’s expansionist policies. We had nothing against ordinary people. If peaceful tourists wanted to come, they were welcome. If someone was doing business without supporting the war, there was no problem.”

According to Tsereteli, maintaining economic and humanitarian ties was part of Georgia’s diplomatic strategy. At the time, there was still hope that international pressure would persuade Russia to honour its commitments.

“There was an attempt to reverse the process after 2008 and encourage Russia, through diplomacy, to fulfil its obligations. That was the rationale behind this policy.”

He adds that Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 fundamentally changed that approach. It demonstrated that the prospects for reaching diplomatic agreements with Moscow had diminished even further.

“The war in Ukraine convinced everyone that there is no longer any real basis for dialogue with Russia.”

Irakli Pavlenishvili makes a similar argument. He says it was important for Georgia after 2008 to show that its conflict was not with the Russian people.

“Because of people like Kobakhidze, who promoted these narratives, we constantly had to explain that we were not fighting Russians, that we were not xenophobic and were not looking for conflict. We could still welcome them as ordinary tourists.”

Pavlenishvili also notes that the previous government faced the opposite criticism at the time. Its opponents accused it of adopting an excessively harsh and xenophobic tone towards Russia.

“The contexts of 2008 and 2022 are different”

Philosopher Levan Gambashidze argues that the biggest flaw in Kobakhidze’s comparison is that it ignores how much the political context has changed. In his view, comparing the post-2008 period with the present day is misleading. Russia’s behaviour has changed, and so has the policy of the Georgian government.

According to Gambashidze, under the previous government there was no widespread perception that the state was pursuing a pro-Russian course.

“There was no sense that we were subordinated to Russia.”

He says the key question is not Kobakhidze’s individual arguments, but his motives. Gambashidze asks who benefits from portraying “Russophobia” as a problem.

“Which country would be concerned about growing ‘Russophobia’ around the world? Russia. Now ask yourself why the Georgian government would be concerned about it.”

According to Gambashidze, since 2022 the authorities have repeatedly warned the public about the possibility of war with Russia. He argues that this has itself contributed to growing fears of Russia.

“If ‘Russophobia’ means fear or hostility towards Russia, and if Georgian Dream has been warning its own population about the possibility of war with Russia since 2022, then what explains the rise in these ‘Russophobic’ sentiments after 2022?”

The Telavi incident

Some of Kobakhidze’s critics also link his statement to a recent confrontation between Georgian citizens and Russian tourists at a wedding in the town of Telavi.

Gigi Tsereteli suggests the statement may have been prompted by the public reaction to that incident. He also says Russia could use such episodes as a pretext to exert political pressure on Georgia.

Grigol Gegelia goes further, arguing that Russian security services could exploit the growing flow of Russian tourists to stage provocations.

“We have long warned that allowing Russians to enter the country without proper controls would end badly. Now Russian intelligence has fertile ground for provocations. It can use these people to carry them out.”

What arguments does Georgian Dream make?

Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party have echoed the main points of Kobakhidze’s statement almost word for word.

“You clearly remember what Saakashvili, Khoshtaria and Japaridze were saying. They unilaterally introduced visa-free travel for Russian citizens, transferred ownership of our strategic assets to Russian state-owned companies, cast the decisive vote in favour of Russia’s accession to the World Trade Organization, welcomed Russian tourists at the border because that was the task they had been given, and became Russophobes only after Russia invaded Ukraine,” said Levan Machavariani, first deputy chair of the Georgian Dream parliamentary faction.

Machavariani also cites rulings by international courts to support the government’s position. He points out that Georgia won legal cases against Russia in Strasbourg and The Hague.

“For us, Russia has been an occupying power since August 2008. It makes no difference what it did later in another country.”

Parliamentary Vice Speaker Nino Tsilosani also argues that the opposition’s attitude changed in line with the international political agenda.

“For years after the August 2008 war, we watched today’s radicals applaud the promotion of Russian tourism and Russian capital instead of protesting against it.”

Tsilosani likewise argues that the opposition’s current rhetoric stems not from Georgia’s own experience but from “instructions from abroad” received after 2022.

“Remaining silent about the suffering of your own people while shouting slogans dictated from abroad is neither patriotism nor genuine solidarity. It is simply unquestioning service to someone else’s interests.”

The opposition’s main question

Some opposition parties do not engage with Kobakhidze’s historical comparisons at all. Instead, they focus on the government’s current policies.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the Gakharia – For Georgia party argues that debating the policies of 2008–2012 cannot replace answers about the ongoing occupation and the risk of annexation.

“Does Irakli Kobakhidze mean that today he should continue the same policy that the United National Movement pursued after 2008? Is he using the United National Movement to justify his own collaboration with Georgia’s main enemy — Russia?”

According to Sharashidze, the current government should be responding to Russia’s actions in the Tskhinvali region and assessing the threat of further integration of the occupied territory.

“What matters is not what happened in 2008. What matters is what is happening today.”

Georgia’s Western course

Kobakhidze’s critics also link his statement to Georgia’s foreign policy. In their view, the prime minister’s text portrays the West, the opposition and civil society — rather than Russia — as the country’s main threats.

According to Gigi Tsereteli, although the previous government made many mistakes, it never abandoned Georgia’s Western course.

Tsereteli argues that Kobakhidze’s statement repeats familiar Russian propaganda narratives, particularly by portraying civil society and Western partners as part of a system of external control.

“I believe the text was, at the very least, edited by people affiliated with the Kremlin.”

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Ahali party, offered an even harsher assessment. In his view, the statement confuses historical facts with political concepts.

“I cannot recall even Bidzina Ivanishvili’s texts containing such a mess, so much slander and falsehood, such confusion of facts, dates and concepts, and, above all, Russophilia on this scale.”

World.title: Katherine residents gather en masse to protest rolling youth crime spree
World.content:
About 50 members of the Katherine community have gathered on the Northern Territory town's main street to express their fear and frustration at the region's crime rate after the latest in a string of car thefts.

It comes after a group of young people were seen driving around the town three hours south of Darwin yesterday, with footage posted to social media showing a black Volkswagen hatchback being driven dangerously for hours until about 9pm, when it eventually crashed on Stutterd Street.

An NT Police spokesperson said in statement "approximately seven" of the occupants were then seen exiting the allegedly stolen car, with investigators later identifying three suspects.

Police in Katherine are investigating after a stolen car was allegedly driven recklessly around the town for several hours before eventually crashing. (ABC News: James Elton)

The spokesperson said police "understood the frustration" of some community members but defended the choice not to initiate a pursuit prior to the crash, saying it could have escalated the situation and put more innocent people at risk.

In response to the incident, local businessman Ben Coutts took to social media this morning, asking residents to attend a planned "coffee with a cop" event at a local cafe to express their frustration with a perceived lack of action on youth crime.

"We need help, the community needs help, we're scared, and we're sick of paying the cost," he told the ABC.

Natalie Ellis says some social media commentary in the wake of the latest incident has been "vicious against Aboriginal people". (ABC News: James Elton)

"We are here as the people of Katherine."

Natalie Ellis, who works on the Katherine Justice Reinvestment project with a cohort of around 20 at-risk youth, said some of the commentary on social media had been "vicious against Aboriginal people".

Ms Ellis asked the community to remember that "95 per cent of the kids in town are good", saying disengagement from school was the number one problem driving youth crime.

"Aboriginal people are victims too, and we need to not forget that," she said.

Police resourcing, curfews raised

The crowd gathered outside the cafe included members of the Katherine Town Council, who stressed they were appearing in their private capacity.

Among them was Toni Tapp Coutts, who said it was time the NT government considered a temporary youth curfew in Katherine like those seen in Alice Springs in recent years.

"I think we should have a curfew, the temperature of the town needs to be lowered," she said.

Toni Tapp Coutts says it is time the NT government considers imposing curfews. (ABC News: James Elton)

"Those kids need to have time to think about their actions, the families need to be forced to confront some of this behaviour in the town, and taking responsibility."

Speaking with community members and local media, NT Police Superintendent Virginia Read suggested there could be a case for more police resources in Katherine.

"If I had my way, it would be nice if we could have some more police," she said.

Member for Katherine Jo Hersey, who was also at the gathering, said she shared the community's frustration and would continue to raise the issue with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro.

Virginia Read says "it would be nice if we could have some more police" on the beat in Katherine. (ABC News: James Elton)

"People are pissed off," she said.

"It's come time now where we do need some more resources in town here."

Ms Hersey said she understood the calls for a curfew but questioned whether it would be effective, saying the curfew in Alice Springs just pushed crime "further out" of the city centre.

But she said she would raise the option of a curfew with Mrs Finocchiaro "if that's what the community wanted".

Mother says she is lucky to be alive

Ashleigh Pugh said she was driving home with her two-year-old daughter yesterday when she had a close encounter with the black Volkswagen.

Ms Pugh said the car was coming towards her head-on, trying to overtake a road train while evading police before veering off the road at the last moment.

"There was absolutely no chance they were going to beat that road train before colliding with me and my daughter, even at the speed they were travelling at," she said.

Police say they have identied three suspects after up to seven youths were seen exiting the Volkswagon after it crashed on Stutterd Street. (ABC News: James Elton)

"I thank God and everything above that at the last second they did that.

"I pulled over, I caught my breath, I bawled my eyes out, and I turned to my girl and I just thanked everything that we were still there."

Mr Pugh said she "used to be proud" to call Katherine home, but no longer felt it was the same town she grew up in.

"Yesterday's incident was yet another key highlight of the seemingly never-ending escalation," she said.

Locals question crime statistics

NT Police crime statistics show overall offending rates in Katherine are down between the 12 months to May this year and the same period last year.

The figures show property crime dropped by 8 per cent while crimes against the person were down 14 per cent — with vehicle thefts the notable exception, rising 21 per cent in the same period.

But long-time locals Jim King and Patty Buntine both said in their view, overall crime was worse now than any time in their memories.

Jeff Usher says locals have "had a gutful" and he has stopped reporting crimes because "nothing happens". (ABC News: James Elton)

Local cabinet-maker Jeff Usher said he had seen repeated break-ins at his workshop, but often did not bother reporting crimes to police because "nothing happens".

"We've had a gutful," he said.

When asked whether Katherine's true crime rate was reflected in the official figures, Ms Hersey said statistics were "one thing" but her experience on the ground was "very different".

"It doesn't pass the pub test," she said.

Jo Hersey says her experience on the ground is "very different" to the picture painted by official statistics. (ABC News: James Elton)

"I absolutely get the anger and the frustration that everyone is feeling, it is absolutely not OK."

Ms Hersey promised to raise the community's frustration at the highest levels of government.

"We do not need any more deaths," she said.

World.title: Do dolphins grieve the way humans do?
World.content:
In a scene akin to a funeral procession, a pod of dolphins surrounds a grieving mother as it nudges along its deceased calf through a picturesque estuary at the bottom end of Western Australia.

The footage was captured by the non-profit conservation group Geographe Marine Research and was initially shared to create awareness of the situation for the coastal community of Bunbury.

It has since attracted thousands of responses from people struck by the seemingly human display of emotion.

The dolphin mother, Fraggle, tried to balance the dead calf on its back as other dolphins joined it in an 11-day "funeral". (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

Geographe Marine Research's Rodney Peterson was behind the drone footage widely shared online, which the organisation uses to monitor the region's frequent marine visitors.

He and the non-profit's head researcher, Capri Jolliffe, said they see dolphins mourning every year.

Do dolphins actually grieve?

The term epimeletic is used by experts to describe animal behaviours like those displayed by Fraggle, the dolphin mother attempting to balance its dead two-week-old calf on her back.

According to Ms Jolliffe the term also extends to acts of caregiving towards sick, injured or dying members in a group.

Experts believe dolphins genuinely experience bouts of grief. (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

She says scientists, while reluctant to attribute human characteristics to animal behaviours, are fairly confident dolphins and other animals are genuinely experiencing bouts of grief "as humans know it" after loss.

According to Ms Jolliffe, animals with high social cognition are recognised as being more intelligent and as a result more "vulnerable to mourning and grief".

Elephants, known for their curiosity and resourcefulness, rely on intricate social hierarchies that lend to epimeletic behaviours like burying deceased herd members, she says.

Whale saved by dolphins A pod of dolphins have guided a stranded juvenile whale out of an estuary.

Researchers have also recorded emotional responses in apes and canines like wolves and dingoes.

Orcas, tooth whales and baleen whales are also known to exhibit epimeletic behaviours.

In particular, dolphins, which do not produce many offspring in their lifetime, invest a lot of energy into the ones they do have and are naturally "highly bonded to their calves", she says.

"Of all the observation of marine mammal species, female dolphins carrying deceased offspring account [for] 75 per cent of recorded cases," Ms Jolliffe says.

How long do dolphins typically mourn?

According to experts, the standard period of time for a dolphin to hold onto their calf typically lasts between three and seven days.

During that time, the pod stays close and checks in on the grieving mother, who is likely to stop feeding altogether.

For Fraggle, the latest loss of the two-week-old calf marks the dolphin's fourth bout of grief after losing its third calf in March last year.

The footage was captured by the non-profit conservation group Geographe Marine Research based in Dunsborough, WA. (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

Mr Peterson says Fraggle was observed with last year's calf for a few days.

Remarkably, this time around, the dolphin held onto its two-week-old calf for 11 days, a period of time Ms Jolliffe says may never have been recorded in dolphins before.

At the end of the period, Fraggle appeared distressed and there were little remains of the calf left.

Despite this, Mr Peterson said Fraggle was back with the pod and a "happy" dolphin again the following day.

Why is this case so remarkable?

Fraggle has always given birth in cooler months and lost all four of its calves in seven years.

The team wonders whether the mother's extensive experience with grief might explain why this period endured longer.

Ocean Census discovers 1,000 species in a year Thousands of species have been discovered lurking and thriving in our oceans.

Mr Peterson also says it might have something to do with slowed decomposition rates which allowed Fraggle to hold on longer.

"You can have your theories," he says.

Either way, as one of the longest observations of a dolphin mother grieving, Ms Jolliffe says the group is hoping the case might be picked up for documentation.

"Dolphins have emotional lives that we don't fully understand," Ms Jolliffe says.

World.title: Live: Lions and Hawks in blockbuster, Cats name player in concussion drama
World.content:
Geelong CEO Steve Hocking has also fronted the media this afternoon to offer some clarity on the whole concussion situation.

Hocking answered a range of questions from reporters and said the club's two-time premiership coach Chris Scott isn't across the matter.

He also revealed that the club has received a 'please explain' letter from the AFL regarding the matter.

Hocking also refused to weigh into the complexity surrounding ex-Cats president Craig Drummond currently being an AFL commission member.

Here's what he said, in part:

"You're looking at that person [who signed off on the waiver] … I take responsibility for the fact we didn't lodge it with the AFL and AFLPA.

"There's no reason [to not lodge the waiver with the AFL], it was just a misstep in the process.

"I'm quite confident [in my position], I've got a board that's very supportive and I'll take full responsibility for it.

"I'm CEO of the Geelong Football Club. We'll work through it over the coming week as we have been over the last couple of days."

"It was conducted for about a two month period. The player's representatives were involved including family and legal representation. That letter spelt out all of that, the entire process," he said.

"It took time, it wasn't rushed, as much as some people believe, that he may have been coerced into it. That is not the case, it was a thorough process.

"The care of the player and getting the player back to play was really important for the football club, for the player and his family.

"The player was very, very clear and involved. There was agency we were looking to achieve and the player still feels that way today, I've dealt with that player today.

"He still feels that care from the club is as strong as ever."

"It was handed back to the football club. From there, it was on us — including our medical officer at the time, the player and all of our board and executive team — to work through that," Hocking said.

"That was a significant process, it was two months of work. It was really important to make sure the player was stepped through his rights and the options that were on the table for him.

"It was about achieving informed consent, as far as the player and his family go."

World.title: Perth business claims $250k loss over Metronet works disruption
World.content:
A Perth business owner says years of railway construction work have cost him hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Joe Mahon says the removal of the Oaks Street Metronet level crossing and subsequent works to elevate the rail line and build a new train station have caused road closures and parking issues that have seriously affected his bottom line.

He told 102.5 ABC Perth he did not object to the public transport upgrades at East Victoria Park from late 2023 to mid-2025, but has asked the Public Transport Authority (PTA) for compensation.

The corner of Bank Street and Forward Street was chosen as the location for Reid's Remotes because of the visibility from the street, customer parking and ease of access.

When Oats Street was subject to closure, it forced prospective customers to access more complicated detours that were subject to frequent change.

"At the start it was gradual because it was issues like their workers taking up all the parking onsite so our customers couldn't actually park," Mr Mahon said.

"Then, once they introduced a road closure, it was like falling off the edge of a cliff. Basically, people couldn't access us.

"The one street that they were supposed to access us through, Forward Street, was full of trucks and cranes and concrete trucks. We even struggled to get there ourselves just to get to work."

The shop was extremely difficult to access at times, Joe Mahon said. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said the sometimes roads were closed during certain times of the day and online maps and GPS services could not keep up.

"Customers would actually give up in frustration and just cancel their booking," he said.

Mr Mahon said in the four years before the level crossing removal works his turnover had been growing by 25 and 30 per cent per annum.

But in the 2024 and 2025 accounting years his turnover fell by 7.45 per cent and 8.75 per cent.

Mr Mahon attributes that decline to the loss of passing trade caused by the Metronet works.

"In 2018 we started documenting every customer who came to us how they found us. One of the main ones is that they're passing trade, so they just saw the signage on the building and came in," he said.

"At the point where the [Metronet] project started that started to decline.

" By about April in 2024 it had gone to zero, and so we had no passing trade for the next 18 months. "

The Metronet worksite on Bank Street, opposite Joe Mahon's business. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said he did not learn that Oats Street would be closed for 18 months until after it was shut.

After the works finished he submitted a compensation claim for $250,000, which he believes his business would have made had it continued to grow at the rate measured before the works began.

The PTA recently denied his claim, saying the changes to traffic conditions were reasonable in the circumstances and undertaken for the benefit of the entire community.

Its legal representatives also said access to the property was continuously maintained and that there was no reasonable alternative way the works could have been carried out.

The PTA also said reasonable steps to mitigate the impact on the community were taken.

But Mr Mahon said he intended to continue his fight for compensation.

"I can't see any other option. I can't afford not to. My business almost closed last year," he said.

"I've sunk the last 19 years into that business.

"I have no problem with the works and the fact that they're essential. I think public transport is essential.

"But when a government department does work that knowingly will impact people and has no consideration for that impact, then that's a problem."

In a statement, a spokesperson for the PTA said: "All claims are assessed on an individual basis. As some claims are still being assessed, details of compensation payments will not be provided."

World.title: Artwork riffing on Renaissance painting and George Orwell wins $100k
World.content:
Ryan Presley, a Marri Ngarr artist from Alice Springs, has taken out the $100,000 top prize at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Awards (NATSIAAs), the longest-running and most prestigious award for Indigenous artists.

Presley — who also has Scandinavian ancestry — won the Telstra Art Award for his oil painting, Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed, a painting of a reclining Indigenous man between his dog and a hunting rifle, which riffs on Renaissance artworks.

Full list of winners Telstra Art Award

Ryan Presley General Painting Award

Vanessa Inkamala Work on Paper Award

Jenna Mayilema Lee Bark Painting Award

Barayuwa Munuŋgurr Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award

Napuwarri Marawili Emerging Artist Award

Guruwuy Murrinyina Multimedia Award

Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri

Measuring 1.8 by 1.5 metres, the painting also speaks to a quote from British author George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past."

Talking to ABC Radio National's Awaye! at the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory in Darwin, Presley described his win as both "daunting" and a "great honour" with which he is still coming to terms.

"It's taken me a while to soak it in," he says.

He says the painting channels representation of sacred spaces and chamber architecture — which can be either a sanctuary or a kind of prison or tomb.

"I want these ideas woven together," he says.

"These are a part of our lives that we negotiate. In Queensland and the Northern Territory, both places I've lived and grown up in, our young people are jailed at alarming rates and at very low ages. That's part of the idea of the work."

Currently based in Logan in south-east Queensland, Presley has worked as an artist for about 20 years, having graduated from Griffith University's contemporary Australian Indigenous art program in 2009.

He has exhibited at Adelaide's Samstag Museum of Art, Melbourne's Gertrude Contemporary and the Institute of Modern Art in Brisbane.

"Basically, I hope [winning] means I'll be able to keep making work," he says.

"I've been working for 17 to 20 years and trying to be consistent and build my work and improve my work, so I'm hoping this helps me continue another 20 years."

2026 NATSIAA finalists on display There's a range of artworks among the finalists vying for this year's National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Awards.

This year's NATSIAAs were judged by Kokatha and Nukunu artist Yhonnie Scarce, Trawlwoolway artist Julie Gough and Kamilaroi artist Warraba Weatherall.

"What caught my attention about Ryan's work is the multi-layered iconography and that story of past, present and, for me, future as well," Scarce says.

"And I think the precision of the painting, the technique of his work, is just next-level amazing."

Presley is one of seven winners, from 64 finalists and 221 entries, at this year's NATSIAAs, including $15,000 awards for general painting, work on paper, bark painting and more.

Blending artistic traditions

In Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed, Presley draws on styles and iconography from throughout art history, including Italian Baroque artist Caravaggio, 16th-century Italian painter Domenico Beccafumi's The Annunciation, and Spanish artist Francisco Goya and his late 18th-century print The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters.

"I'm threading together several well-known works," Presley explains.

Presley created Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed over a period of about six months. (Supplied: MAGNT/Katherine Travis)

He wanted to imitate how those artworks use light, shade, and strong contrasts between the two — a technique known as chiaroscuro.

"The work pushed the boundaries of my skills," he says.

But the painting is more than an act of mimicry.

Presley says he wanted to "reinterpret" those classic works for modern Australia, including by incorporating a bushfire that blazes in the distance.

In his version, Presley affords the Indigenous figure and Australian landscape the "importance, reverence or magnificence" of the subjects of Renaissance paintings, while also drawing a link between the "flourishing" art scene of that period and Aboriginal artists working today.

Presley is also heavily influenced by other First Nations artists, including Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, Albert Namatjira, Gordon Bennett, Fiona Foley, Judy Watson, Gordon Hookey and Richard Bell.

That broad range of influences reaches back to his childhood growing up in Alice Springs and the artists he's worked beside since moving to south-east Queensland.

"[Alice Springs and Brisbane] both definitely shaped me and my world view and what I hold dear and treasure," he says.

"You get a real sense of spirit, cultural survival and transmission to the next generations [from this exhibition]," NATSIAA judge Julie Gough says. (Supplied: MAGNT/Charlie Bliss)

A three-time NATSIAA finalist, after being exhibited in 2016 and 2020, Presley is following in the footsteps of his uncle and fellow artist Laurie Presley, who was a finalist in 2007.

"That was really inspirational to me," he says. "[I thought] if he can do it, maybe I can do it too."

Now, Presley is proud to join the ranks of past winners, with their work over decades demonstrating the vitality of Aboriginal art and artists.

"Aboriginal people make the most important work in Australia, in my opinion," he says.

'A little act of defiance'

Larrakia, KarraJarri and Wardaman artist Jenna Mayilema Lee won the $15,000 Work on Paper Award for her work Taking back taken, in which she weaved dilly bags from paper maps stolen from the British Museum in London.

Lee attended the NATSIAAs as a child, growing up in a family of artists, including her uncle, former NATSIAA winner Gary Lee. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The project grew from the time Canberra-born Lee — who also has Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Irish, and Scottish ancestry — spent living in London in 2019, where she would visit museums and ask to see their collections of stolen Aboriginal artefacts.

Visting the British Museum one day, she noticed the museum's map of its galleries and facilities cost a suggested donation of 2 British pounds.

"I thought that was really cheeky: to suggest that the world can access their culture here, but in order to find out where it is, please give us 2 pounds," she says.

" So, I just decided to take one without paying as a little act of defiance. "

When she got home that evening, she realised the map could become material for her art.

Over the next year, she returned to the museum to nick more maps to turn into Taking back taken, before she moved back to Australia during the pandemic.

From Australia, she recruited family and friends visiting London to steal maps for her.

"I ended up with this network of people who were pinching maps from the British Museum on my behalf, which is not dissimilar to the way that Empire sent people out to collect world culture," Lee says.

"The act of taking it was the work."

Lee has exhibited at Setouchi Trienniale in Japan, the TarraWarra Biennial and as part of Melbourne Now at the NGV. (Supplied: MAGNT/Katherine Travis)

It took about five years for Lee to work up the skill to turn the maps into dilly bags — which she created in the style of the traditional objects she would visit in both local and international museum collections.

"[Taking back taken] is the culmination of a number of years, and of that singular moment of realising that I'd just taken material from the British Museum and that there the opportunity to turn it into something," she says.

It also seemingly builds on work Lee created for the 2020 NATSIAAs, titled HIStory Vessels, which landed her that year's Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award.

Responding to the 250th anniversary of James Cook landing in Australia, Lee used the pages of a Ladybird history book titled The Story of Captain Cook to make a series of objects, including woven bags.

Turning paper into string for weaving is a difficult process — one Lee ascribes to her "sheer stubbornness" as well as to her urge to make work from plant fibres.

But, as an artist working in Melbourne, not on Country, she doesn't have access to the traditional materials used for weaving.

"If I wanted to be a weaver, I had to really think about what I was weaving," she says.

"But if I took a step back and looked around my own home and my own environment, it was just covered in books and paper.

"If I'm following the ways of my ancestors, it's being an expert in the resources around you — these are just the resources around me."

The NATSIAA exhibition is at Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory, Darwin, until January 24.

World.title: Nicole Kidman delivers message to former school on 150th anniversary
World.content:
Lane Cove Public School on Sydney's Lower North Shore has been celebrating its 150th anniversary, and among the former students invited to participate was Academy Award-winner Nicole Kidman.

Birthday celebrations culminated in an open day on Friday during which former students and teachers were welcomed back to the school grounds to mark the occasion.

Hundreds gathered including former teachers and alumni. (Supplied: In the Cove, Jack Kelly)

Kidman responded with a message from her location in Santorini, Greece.

ABC News was on the ground to hear her congratulate the school on 150 years in a recording played out in the hall.

"I wish I could be with you," Kidman said.

"I remember running around that playground.

" I made friends that I'm still friends with now … and I'm so grateful that I went to such a great school. "

Kidman had previously told Network 10 she was going to try to make it to the celebrations after being invited there by students who posted a video encouraging her to turn up.

"It's the sweetest thing ever," Kidman told Angela Bishop.

Former teachers and alumni gather

The event attracted hundreds of people including former teachers and alumni, among them Channel Nine presenter Peter Overton who was a school captain in 1977.

Lane Cove Public School alumnus Peter Overton was quizzed by current students. (Supplied: In the Cove, Jack Kelly)

"You know when I first came here? 55 years ago," Overton said.

"I have so many happy memories of this school."

Overton reeled off the names of teachers he remembered, saying he was lucky to have attended the primary school.

Overton told the audience his good friend Kidman wanted to be there.

"Happy birthday from Nicole," he said.

Meredith Lucas, who was one of Kidman's classmates, returned to the school for the celebrations.

Nicole Kidman (front row, sixth from left) with fellow students including Meredith Lucas (first from left in front row). (Supplied: Lane Cove Public School)

Ms Lucas attended Lane Cove Public School from 1973–1979, from kindergarten to year six, alongside Kidman.

"It was a very close knit school and community and we sang in the choir together," Ms Lucas said.

"I applaud her for all her successes.

"She's a natural talent, she's a hard worker, she came from a good family and a good community.

"And I have watched her career from afar and I feel like she's done amazingly well in a very tough environment, being film and media."

Lane Cove Public School principal Terry McKinnon said he was proud of current and former students, including Kidman.

He said the birthday message she sent arrived just in time.

"It came in very late today and we were very happy to play it," Mr McKinnon said.

"It's great to hear from all our alumni, but particularly Nicole after we invited her to this event.

"We're extremely proud of her, as we are of all our alumni."

The school's official birthday fell on January 14.

It has been around since 1876 and prides itself on its creative arts and music programs.

World.title: China accused as Pacific nations block statement condemning missile test
World.content:
Naoero and Kiribati have stirred frustration at a sometimes tense meeting of Pacific foreign ministers by blocking a regional statement criticising China's recent ballistic missile test, with New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters suggesting Beijing was seeking to influence the gathering.

Both Australia and New Zealand flagged they would push for Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) foreign ministers to make the region's opposition to the test clear, after Pacific nations failed to reach a consensus in its aftermath last month.

But sources from multiple PIF nations have told the ABC that Kiribati and Naoero (formerly Nauru), which have both developed close ties with Beijing in recent years, continued to block consensus on the statement during today's meeting in Suva, despite broad support for it in the room.

Mr Peters was frustrated after the meeting, saying "two countries" — which he did not name — had effectively blocked the joint statement.

"They were seeking to use the need for consensus as a veto provision," he said.

"We made it clear that wasn't the Pacific way."

Winston Peters was frustrated at the Pacific Islands Forum meeting in Fiji. (Supplied)

He also said those two countries were "responding to [an] outside partner's wishes" — although he did not name China.

"We made it very clear that we didn't think outsiders should be telling insiders — that's us, we've been here for thousands of years — what our position should be," he said.

And he declared the two countries blocking the statement "didn't actually lay out any reasons" for their opposition, "apart from their disagreement", saying their position had "no logic".

An official from one PIF nation was even more scathing in private, calling Kiribati's position "absurd" and accusing the country of "lecturing" ministers about the importance of consensus while ignoring the sentiment in the room.

An official from one PIF nation called Kiribati's position "absurd" and accused the country of "lecturing". (Supplied)

Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong also pressed the meeting to issue a joint statement on the test, telling Pacific ministers that they needed to display "leadership" on the issue.

Senator Wong also pressed the meeting to issue a joint statement on the test, telling Pacific ministers that they needed to display "leadership" on the issue.

In a statement, the foreign minister said there had been a "clear and powerful discussion about the responsibility we all share to safeguard peace, stability and security in our region".

Penny Wong implored Pacific leaders to display leadership. (Supplied)

She also pointed out that several Pacific countries had already issued their own statements criticising the missile test.

"The majority of Pacific leaders have spoken loudly and clearly about their concerns regarding China's ballistic missile test, including the importance of respect for sovereignty, transparency and notification," she said.

" I hope that message is heard. "

"In the Pacific way, Australia will continue engaging constructively with all members as we work together on the issues that matter to our region."

The final PIF Foreign Ministers Meeting communique looks set to remain entirely silent on the missile test, although the ABC has been told that all PIF members have agreed to keep on discussing the issue in the hope they can reach an agreement before the PIF Leaders' Meeting in Palau in early September.

World.title: Concerns planned boot camps may allow child abuse to go unreported
World.content:
Child welfare and rights agencies across Australia have condemned Queensland's proposed youth offender boot camps, delivering repeated warnings that children as young as 10 would be at risk of harm or abuse at the facilities.

Compounding their concern is the fact that the Queensland government proposes to give boot camp operators a "reasonable excuse" under the legislation not to report any harm to a child, if doing so would tend to incriminate them.

The Youth Justice (Circuit Breaker) Amendment Bill 2026 was introduced in the state parliament on June 25 and referred to the Justice, Integrity and Community Safety Committee for detailed consideration. The committee will table its report to parliament next week.

Sue-Anne Hunter says child abuse will go unreported in these boot camps. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Sue-Anne Hunter, the National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, said it was "outrageous" that harm to children in Queensland's proposed youth offender boot camps could go unreported.

"This bill just does not make sense," she said.

"I'm just gobsmacked … the more I look into it."

More than half of children in youth detention in Queensland are indigenous.

"We've got these children that are out of the way," Ms Hunter said.

"No-one has eyes on them. Anything can happen to them and nobody actually has to report [harm]."

Under the government's Circuit Breaker Program, part of a pre-election commitment by the Crisafulli government, children who would otherwise be detained on bail or sentenced to youth detention would instead be sent by a court to one of two remote properties with a service provider for up to six months.

Participants would be required to wear an electronic monitoring device and would be given basic education and hands-on learning in agriculture and livestock management.

Minister for Youth Justice Laura Gerber has described the program as an "intensive rehabilitation program for repeat youth offenders, designed to drive down youth crime".

In a statement, the Department of Youth Justice said it would oversee this program.

"The Department will be responsible for oversight of the program, including monitoring provider performance, compliance, and outcomes," the spokesperson said.

However, Ms Hunter said the children in these camps would have fewer safeguards than would apply in a youth detention centre.

"We know what happens to children in closed institutions a long way from anywhere, where the child depends entirely on adults controlling their day and nobody independent is walking through the door unannounced," she said.

"We know it because of previous royal commissions in this country. And every one of those institutions was well intentioned on paper.

"What we're saying is ... you can do whatever you want to these children that are hundreds of miles away from anybody, anywhere.

"They don't have access to family, community, kin and culture — and they're there for six months."

Child harm kept under wraps

Legal Aid Queensland says the protections against self-incrimination in the bill are alarming. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Legal Aid Queensland acting chief executive Nicky Davies said they were "deeply troubled" by protection against self-incrimination.

"If a child suffers harm while participating in the provider's Circuit Breaker Program, it will almost always likely incriminate the reporting entity in some way," wrote acting chief executive Nicky Davies in her submission to the parliamentary inquiry into the legislation.

All other organisations that care for children in the state, including child care centres, schools and hospitals, are required to report complaints to the Queensland Family and Child Commission under what is called the Reportable Conduct Scheme. This includes incidents of sexual abuse or exploitation, physical abuse, significant neglect, or emotional harm that causes significant harm to the child.

Abuse will go unreported

Luke Twyford says any harm to a child needs to be reported, documented and investigated. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Queensland Family and Child Commission's principal commissioner Luke Twyford said he was confused how the program could allow bootcamp operators a "reasonable excuse" not to report harm.

Mr Twyford said he was not satisfied that if children in remote bush camps were harmed, it would be reported to authorities.

"I think the short answer is very clearly no," he said in an interview with 612 ABC Brisbane.

Child safeguards rendered weak

Meanwhile, the Office of the Public Guardian, Queensland, has cautioned it does not have the resources to guarantee the oversight of the remote bush camps under its community visitor program, as envisaged in the legislation.

"Community visitor oversight is a critical safeguard for children at circuit breaker sites," noted public guardian Shayna Smith in her submission to a parliamentary inquiry into the legislation.

However, she said the cost of visiting remote locations and the likely increase in complaints due to mandatory electronic monitoring and family separation meant, "without additional resources, OPG is concerned oversight may be diluted".

Under the legislation, the chief executive of the Youth Justice Department could dismiss complaints about the treatment and welfare of children at remote boot camps if they were deemed to be "trivial or made only to cause annoyance".

Ms Smith said dismissing grievances as "annoying" undermined a child's right to be heard.

"At a minimum, written reasons for dismissing complaints should be provided … with review pathways available," she said.

The bill also fails to set minimum standards of care for children, such as accommodation, food, health services, disability support, family contact, cultural support or reintegration planning, Ms Smith noted.

Her submission also said the bill failed to specify necessary health and safety standards given the children would be required to participate in "hands-on" learning at isolated agricultural properties, she warned.

However, in a statement, the Department of Youth Justice said providers would be held to legal standards.

"Providers will be required to meet minimum standards and legislative obligations relating to the care, education, wellbeing, and support of young people," the spokesperson said.

In late June, the Department of Youth Justice sought urgent interest from rural or remote working properties, "like cattle stations", to operate residential programs "in a remote secure 24/7 facility".

There is no specific requirement in the legislation for the children to undergo a physical or mental health assessment prior to being recommended as suitable for placement at a remote bush camp, in order to tailor a program to meet their needs.

According to the Legal Aid Queensland submission to the inquiry, of the children engaged with the youth justice system, about 44 per cent have a diagnosed or suspected mental health.

A similar proportion likely have a disability, 55 per cent are First Nations and 48 per cent have been disengaged from education.

It also highlighted that many had experienced housing insecurity. More than half had a history of trauma, having experienced or been impacted by domestic and family violence.

Ms Hunter, a trained social worker, said this background made them vulnerable to being victimised by adults and other children, particularly as the remote camps would host boys and girls ranging in age from 10 to 17.

"Overwhelmingly [these] children have already themselves been harmed," she said.

"[No-one is asking] do they have autism, ADHD, fetal alcohol syndrome?

"What looks like a child refusing to comply is often a child with a cognitive disability, a communication difference, a trauma response or some sort of impairment [displaying] a response they cannot control."

She said the bill was not based on a therapeutic model.

"It does not guarantee the child mental health care or a disability assessment, trauma-informed practice, alcohol and drug treatment or family therapy," Ms Hunter said.

"Given who these children are, those things are not extras. They are the entire point.

"Discipline and livestock handling are not [what] these kids need.

" They are being set up to fail. "

A violation of human rights

Deb Tsorbaris says the proposed boot camps will not be beneficial for youth offender rehabilitation. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

National Children's Commissioner Deb Tsorbaris said the scheme would breach Commonwealth and Queensland's own human rights law and must be abandoned.

"It's unacceptable," she said, speaking on 612 ABC Brisbane.

" And frankly, it will not work. These boot camps have been proven not to work. "

A similar program devised by then attorney general and current Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleije in 2013 was later scrapped by the Palaszczuk government in 2015 after an independent report by KPMG found 63.5 per cent of participating young people reoffended and the program was no more effective at stopping crime than standard youth detention.

Expressions of interest have now closed for private providers to apply for a share of the $80 million budget to run the two boot camps.

That document indicated the government wants 10 children sent to the first boot camp up by September 1, with the second camp operating by the second quarter of 2027.

However, legislation to establish the boot camps has yet to pass the Queensland Parliament.

Youth minister tight-lipped

Laura Gerber has repeatedly turned down 612 ABC's requests for an interview. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber has declined repeated requests for an interview to clarify whether the government will amend or abandon the scheme.

The Queensland Human Rights Commission, which oversees the operation of the Queensland Human Rights Act, has not made a submission to the parliamentary inquiry into the legislation.

Nor has it made any specific, public comment about the Circuit Breaker Program.
