World.title: Cheap parking could go at Melbourne Zoo as Royal Park masterplan revealed
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCity life Cheap parking could go at Melbourne Zoo as Royal Park masterplan revealed Angelica Snowden August 7, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capped daily car park rates of $2 at the Melbourne Zoo could be abolished to encourage public transport travel under a new Royal Park masterplan. After key community and environmental groups criticised a draft proposal for the 161-hectare inner-city park, including proposals for increased lighting and more sports ovals, a revised pitch was published by the council on Friday afternoon before a meeting on August 18. Jill and Todd Watson took son Max, 10 months, to the zoo on Friday. The Royal Park masterplan suggests removing the $2 daily cap for parking there. Justin McManus One of the proposals most likely to prove contentious is to lobby the state government to remove the parking fee cap at the zoo. “Parking around the zoo is capped at a daily fee of $2, based on state government legislation from 1985,” the masterplan said. “Low parking fees encourage people to use private vehicles and discourage public transport, thereby entrenching the need for internal roads and car parks.”



Lord Mayor Nick Reece said changes to the zoo parking cap would need to be voted on by the council. “Anything to do with parking will be done in a sensitive and strategic way,” he said. Matt Golding “I am also keenly aware that there are eight hectares of bitumen parking in Royal Park and, if we are smart, we can liberate a lot of that, get good parking outcomes and create new green space.” Jill and Todd Watson, who visited Melbourne Zoo with their 10-month-old son Max on Friday, said it was disappointing to learn the council might abolish the parking cap. “As a family, we travel with a pram, and it is more practical to drive,” Jill Watson said. “Going to the zoo is a family-friendly activity and should be accessible.”



She pointed out the cost of visiting the zoo was $58 for a one-off visit, or $150 for membership. “We paid $300 today on our first visit,” she said, after they each bought a membership. “I can see both sides, though. I understand the need for planning to encourage the use of public transport.” According to the masterplan, the council is considering acquiring nearby land to increase the footprint of the city’s prized nature reserve. Where suitable land adjacent to the park is offered for sale, the City of Melbourne will consider strategic land acquisition to increase the size of the park, the plan says. The council is eyeing land bounded by Oak and Park streets, in the city’s inner north, currently occupied by the Melbourne Youth Justice Centre, global biotech company CSL’s former headquarters and the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Paul Leitinger is convener of the Royal Park Protection Group Justin McManus



“We must be nimble to capture these opportunities when they arise, with a particular focus on land bounded by Oak and Park streets, which historically formed part of the park,” the masterplan said. The land where the old CSL headquarters sits is now owned by the Victorian government, after the company relocated in 2023 to Elizabeth Street. The council has proposed to limit artificial light in the park to improve night sky viewing and adopt “strict lighting curfews to minimise impacts on biodiversity”. Lighting should be used only up to 10.30pm to maintain a dark park between 10.30pm and 5am, under the plan, except for walking and cycling thoroughfares and major destinations within the park. These include the State Netball and Hockey Centre, the zoo, Royal Park station and tram stops.



The masterplan also noted it was “challenging to reduce lighting to minimise impacts on wildlife, while maintaining perceptions of safety”. The council plans to register the park as an Urban Night Sky Place with the International Dark Sky Association by ensuring that areas deemed suitable or designated as “dark sky refugia (for example, the Grassland Circle and the golf course) remain unlit for the duration of the night”. Related Article City life When pedestrians rebel: What desire paths tell us about the city Royal Park Protection Group convener Paul Leitinger welcomed the masterplan revisions, including plans to keep Royal Park dark. “The lighting issues are a great advancement,” he said.



“In the original plan they had crisscrossed the whole park with paths of desire, new walking tracks going all over the place carving up the park. We objected to that because you want to be in the wilderness.” The masterplan also paves the way for more sports ovals, but they will be subject to a framework to evaluate their necessity. The plan aims to avoid further expansion of major sport facilities in the park while increasing the capacity of existing sports grounds by extending operating hours, particularly in winter. Leitinger said he hoped criteria to evaluate the installation of new ovals would uphold the values of the park as a green space. “We must have the full support of the council, and I suppose the Victorian government, to uphold those principles and apply them,” he said. Protectors of Public Lands Victoria president Fiona Bell has previously opposed the construction of new sports grounds at an area known as lawn seven. According to the revised masterplan, the area will be turned into a formal sporting zone.



Fiona Bell and other resident and community groups have expressed concern about plans to add sporting grounds. Jason South Reece said the revised masterplan addressed concerns of community and environmental groups and would deliver “more park for more people”. Addressing concerns about lawn seven, Reece said no new sporting facilities would be constructed in the area, but it would be “utilised” for formal activities. “The balanced approach we are taking in this masterplan is to say lawn seven will have work done on it, so it is more usable as a sporting area. But we are going to do it in a sensitive way,” he said. Overall, the masterplan proposes increasing the physical green space of the park by reducing street level car parking and removing roads.



Car parking bays in Royal Park could be moved to the outer section of the park. There are 3087 above-ground parking bays, many of which could be replaced by possible underground parking at the zoo and State Netball and Hockey Centre to preserve precious outdoor space for biodiversity and recreation, according to the masterplan. Reece said safety was a top priority for the park. “We have moved away from the concept of a uniformly dark park, to a balanced, zoned lighting framework. Key pathways and destinations can be appropriately lit with environmentally sensitive areas to remain darker to protect wildlife,” he said. World.title: Sydney can change while preserving its treasures
World.content:
NationalNSWNote From The Editor Sydney can change while preserving its treasures Jordan Baker August 7, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I have long felt a sense of unease about the renovation of North Sydney Olympic Pool. It was less about the astronomical budget ($122 million) and five-year closure – although this has certainly concerned many of our readers – than about what the wrecking ball might do to this art deco treasure, which I have always considered one of Sydney’s most beautiful public facilities. North Sydney Olympic Pool reopened this morning after a five-year closure. Sam Mooy My attachment is unashamedly emotional: North Sydney was my childhood pool. I remember racing down the iconic staircase to get to squad training, eating red icy poles on the pool deck and cheering from the grandstand at school swimming carnivals. We’d leap from the diving boards, nag Mum for a coin for hot showers, and swim beneath the “bubble” (a strange temporary tent) in winter. I loved it for its beauty, its familiarity and its sense of history. I didn’t want it to change. As North Sydney Mayor Zoe Baker said at the opening celebration, “Everyone owns their local pool. We each carry stories and memories.” But Sydney, as Premier Chris Minns often says, is not a museum. It must change. We need more housing, and our social infrastructure, such as our pools, must evolve to meet the needs of new and younger residents.



This doesn’t mean we must unquestioningly throw all the city’s gems on the pyre of progress. Sydney can change while still preserving its treasures. To do this we should be able to have constructive, nuanced and frank public discussions – and we do, in the pages of the Herald – about what’s special enough to keep, what we should adapt and what we must sacrifice. We can do this without either side of the debate resorting to reductive monikers such as “YIMBY” or “NIMBY”. Mayor Zoe Baker addresses the crowd during the reopening of the pool. Sam Mooy We’re having that debate about Victoria Barracks in Paddington and HMAS Penguin in Mosman. The defence department is selling them off, sparking tension between those who believe these sites could host more housing while preserving their heritage, and others who believe these sites are too special to touch. Minns on Friday announced a major rezoning of North Parramatta that will provide thousands of homes. He says the plan preserves the historic Female Factory; others fear the housing comes too close to one of Australia’s most significant women’s convict sites. There will never be consensus but constructive, open-minded debate that remains mindful of the need for Sydney to be a liveable, affordable and welcoming city is our best path to a practical compromise. Which brings me back to North Sydney Pool. I visited on Friday morning and my hopes were low. I feared it would be a $122 million exercise in desecration. Certainly, attempts in other parts of Sydney to combine history preservation and functionality – such as the awkward renovation of the city’s first freshwater pool at Enfield, for example (which is now being renovated again) – ended up achieving neither.



At first glimpse my prejudices were affirmed. The beautiful red brick wall that used to line the street was overshadowed by a boxy, light grey building. But upon closer inspection, the wall was still there and the box housed a pristine new indoor program pool, complete with sauna and steam room. (I would have faked illness less frequently if my winter swimming squad had been held there rather than in the bubble.) The old grandstand with concrete cancer might have been replaced by a new one but its view of the harbour is just as magnificent. The art deco arches have been preserved. Sam Mooy The art deco arches have been preserved, and while the children’s pool has been enlarged, the tiles still use the old pattern. The sun deck has been reconstructed using the original red bricks. I would have liked the change rooms to be preserved – I loved the old fittings, even if it meant the bathrooms were freezing – but most pool users will prefer the new comforts, which include heated floors and a machine I’ve never seen before, to spin water out of wet cozzies. The pool might no longer be the one at which I created my childhood memories but it will be a place for our children to create their own. It has been an expensive exercise, and a chaotic one. The saga has been extensively documented by our Sydney editor Megan Gorrey, who wrote on Friday about how the project became a lightning rod for debate about whether local governments should embark on such large infrastructure projects as councils across Sydney struggle to upgrade pools.



The council’s finances are in disarray because of it, and rates will be hiked to help pay for it. Still, Zoe Baker believes visitors will be won over by the “absolutely beguiling” venue. Loading It will be up to North Sydney ratepayers to decide if the cost, delays and debt have been worth it. The pool is free to visit this weekend but for those who can’t make it down to Milsons Point – or think it’s too cold! – our video team has produced a video. Cindy Yin, who also had her school swimming carnivals at North Sydney, has written a review. Her view is that despite the huge budget and construction delays, the thing that made North Sydney a great pool – its extraordinary location – has not changed. She writes: “As other councils embark on their own pool renovations across Sydney, I hope they remember what actually matters to most people: welcoming, accessible places to swim, built on time and on budget.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Live: NZ Warriors v Penrith Panthers,  NRL
World.content:
Follow all the NRL action, as the Warriors take on the Penrith Panthers at Go Media Stadium.

Kickoff is at 8pm.

The Warriors are again preparing to measure themselves against the NRL's benchmark, as they begin their run to the post-season.

Last time the Warriors met the NRL leaders, the top-of-the-table contest was acclaimed as a worthy dress rehearsal for October's grand final.

Without their Origin stars, the two teams ran each other to a standstill, splitting possession 50/50 and completing sets at a combined 91 percent (71/78), before the Panthers emerged 20-18 winners.

While they walked away from Sydney's Commbank Stadium empty-handed, the Warriors lost no respect across the competition, but a 3-4 record over the next two months has since seen them slide from second on the ladder.

Coach Andrew Webster is philosophical about that result.

"We were there to achieve two points," he reflected. "If we had won, that was an extra two points for our tally.

"I'm not sure losing it was more beneficial, but I know we gained some clarity from that game on what we need to do to be better."

World.title: Winston Peters says Pacific missed chance to issue statement after Chinese missile test
World.content:
Foreign Minister Winston Peters says the Pacific missed an opportunity not to issue a joint statement soon after China launched a nuclear-capable missile into waters near Tuvalu.

He spoke before Friday's Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers' Meeting where the ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China. Peters had earlier labelled it a "delicate issue".

Peters is in Fiji for the meeting along with counterparts from 17 other Pacific countries, in preparation for the leaders' meeting in Palau, in early September.

It's been a month since China test-launched a nuclear-capable ballistic missile with a dummy warhead into the Pacific Ocean - a nuclear free zone.

It was met with condemnation from some Pacific leaders, and Christopher Luxon said the New Zealand government made clear to China that the move was unacceptable - but there has not been a unanimous statement from Pacific nations.

Peters said New Zealand had been pushing for one.

Peters - who did not name the countries - said they were granting outside partners' wishes rather than those of the Pacific Islands Forum.

"So we made it very clear that we do not think that outsiders should be telling the insiders - that's us [who] have been here for thousands of years - what our position should be, and it's an ongoing piece of work at this piece of time."

"It's a very delicate issue," he said, suggesting some countries would come to the meeting with their minds made up.

"The roadblock is that if you've had a predetermined position, any discussion here and any logic and reasoning will not land," he said.

"We'll see whether logic prevails in this debate, or whether the debate has already been settled by people having a predetermined position from which they will not move."

The PIF Foreign Leaders' Meeting group photo in Fiji on 7 August 2026. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

He said it was not too late to take a joint position however it should have been done sooner: "the sooner the better."

The countries should not be in a position where they could not reach consensus on the matter, said Peters.

"At this point in time, we've got one third of the world's surface, there's a desperation for serious funds when it comes to resilience building in this part of the world," he said.

"The economic situation is not good, so we need each other more than ever, and we need international recognition as well more than ever."

Peters had a brief discussion with Australia's foreign minister Penny Wong on Friday morning ahead of the meeting, but would not say whether the two countries were on the same page.

He said there would also be discussion about how partner countries work with PIF following the controversial decision to ban them - including heavy hitters like China and the US - from last year's meeting in the Solomon Islands.

Peters has spoken out repeatedly about "outsiders" influencing the Solomon Islands Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele to implement the ban, which Manele denied, arguing the block made sense while PIF leaders considered how best to respond to the increasing interest from partners wanting a seat at the regional decision-making table.

"We need their help," Peters said.

"This idea of tiering people and all sorts of this part of the discussion, if it means that you actually lose the chance for buy-in by serious countries, then that'll be a big mistake."

Fiji's foreign minister Sakiasi Ditoka opened the meeting with a call for unity.

"Even as our strategic environment becomes more complex, the Pacific response should not be fragmentation or division," he said, as the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Minister's meeting kicked off.

"It should be greater regional solidarity, stronger consensus and continued confidence in our own regional institutions and processes."

He said the foreign ministers had a "unique responsibility," helping to shape how the Pacific "engages the world, manages these partnerships, and protects the integrity of our regional institutions".

Ditoka said the matters before the forum reflect that responsibility, from "strengthening our peace and security architecture", to advancing the 2050 "international engagement strategy" and "deepening regional integration".

He also stated it was about "ensuring our partnerships continue to serve Pacific priorities".

"Together they represent practical steps towards implementing the vision set out in the 2050 strategy for the blue Pacific continent."

The secretary general Baron Waqa followed, saying guidance from the foreign ministers would continue to shape the evolution of regionalism and the "trajectory of regional institutions".

For his part, he said, "allow me to reaffirm that the secretariat remains committed to supporting a forum that is increasingly strategic" and responsible.

"One that is able to anticipate emerging challenges, coordinate regional action, and deliver effectively on the priorities set by leaders."

Meanwhile, Tuvalu's foreign secretary Pasuna Tuaga said his country had asked for help searching for the dummy warhead, which landed in nearby waters.

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum fails to reach consensus on anti-missile statement against China
World.content:
Disagreement from some China-aligned Pacific Islands countries has prevented regional countries within the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) issuing a joint statement against missile testing in the Pacific.

At their meeting in Suva on Friday, PIF foreign ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China after it fired a nuclear-capable missile into Pacific waters last month, despite deep concern among most countries about Beijing's actions.

It is understood there was a majority of countries represented at the meeting who wanted a clear joint regional statement condemning such missile testing in the nuclear-free Pacific.

However, the Forum's usual Pacific decision-making by consensus could not be met because Kiribati and Nauru were opposed to a strong statement condemning the testing.

New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters told media some Pacific nations were using the consensus because they were more concerned with external partners' wishes than those that belong to the Pacific Islands Forum, something he described as an "unusual view".

"They didn't actually lay out any reasons, apart from their disagreement, and not wishing for us to make the clear statement such as 'we are opposed to missiles being fired into the Pacific'.

"That's what the statement should have said, and we're still waiting for that to get laid out."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters speaking to reporters in Fiji ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Ministers' meeting on Friday. Supplied / screenshot

Some governments have pointed out that China is not the only country testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific. The US regularly conducts tests into the Marshall Islands.

Peters pointed out that testing in the Marshall Islands was done with the country's consent.

Security agenda

The PIF Foreign Ministers Meeting was held to set the agenda for the annual Leaders' Meeting in Palau later this month.

A Solomon Islands proposal for a regional security treaty was one of the discussion points, although it's clear more consultation is required on the matter.

The Solomon Islands' Foreign Affairs and External Trade permanent secretary George Hoa'au RNZ Pacific that there was already a range of regional security mechanisms in the Forum fale.

"The missing part is to have a common thatched roof over them," he said.

"The proposal for this single security treaty by Solomons is to provide an umbrella on top of what is already regional MOUs which are non-binding."

World.title: Bad week? Try being a Chris
World.content:
Analysis: It's been a rough week in politics and if it's not one Chris having a bad day, it's the other.

That was the case on Friday when four shocker days for the prime minister swung to the left following a woeful poll result for Labour's Chris Hipkins.

Christopher Luxon's foot-in-mouth moments would have been enough on their own without adding in his foreign minister telling a Chinese-Kiwi Parliamentary colleague to "go back to where you've come from", and unemployment at an 11-year high, with just 92 days until the election.

A sympathetic observer would look to Luxon's time at the helm and say he's had bad luck with being handed a complicated coalition, an economy on its knees, and an unpredictable US president.

Yet, Luxon is the first to ignore the complexities of Covid - a worldwide pandemic never seen in our time - and the problems that created for Labour and Jacinda Ardern.

So, on that basis his starting point for all prime ministers is that regardless of the crisis - health or economic or both - it's not an excuse for the government of the day's performance, or lack thereof.

That's a problematic baseline for a governing party that sold itself as the economic fixer.

While there are plenty of improvements to be celebrated - turning points in some (not all) business confidence, inflation at times getting closer to the target bracket - there are also some nightmare numbers Luxon cannot ignore.

Christopher Luxon. Pool/AFP/Michael Bradley

The biggest one came this week in the form of an unemployment rise to an 11-year high of 5.6 percent.

There are now 171,000 people unemployed and around 8000 more people are experiencing long term unemployment - those out of work for a year or more - this June quarter than in the same quarter last year.

Couple that with Luxon's brainfart moment last weekend where he decided to attack provincial New Zealand small and medium sized businesses (SMEs) telling them they had a "parent-child mentality" and needed to be more "adult" and the prime minister's grip on the economy doesn't look so tight.

Former National Party leader turned Auckland Business Chamber chief executive Simon Bridges summed it up best in a NZ Herald column on Friday morning.

"And to state what I hope is blindingly obvious, but clearly isn't, SMEs are very different from a business with thousands of employees and hundreds of millions or billions in turnover. They didn't, as the Prime Minister says he did, "sit in Illinois for six years" as an executive of consumer goods company Unilever, and they don't think that much about "commercially superior returns, great customer experience and awesome internal culture". Not explicitly anyway. The owner very often is the internal culture, the HR manager, accounts, marketing and everything else, rolled into one. They are busy just surviving. They do their best every day without huge analysis or much if any support.

"Yet, such lowly businesspeople do worry about what the Government does, because the Government in this small nation controls so much in terms of spending, sentiment, policies and programmes. Its taxes, costs and red tape make all the difference, as do its statements and initiatives," Bridges wrote.

It's a scathing reality check for the prime minister who prides himself on getting out of the Wellington bubble and connecting with everyday Kiwis living in the region to find himself managing to offend, and later having to apologise to, what was considered a friendly business audience.

NZ First leader Winston Peters and Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan. RNZ

Supporters have commended Luxon for acknowledging he got it wrong and saying sorry, but there are others who have asked how he stuffed it up in the first place.

The point Luxon was trying to make about him wanting government to get out of the way so that business can thrive is valid, but despite making this point on so many occasions in the past two-and-a-half years to various business audiences he still hasn't nailed the delivery of it.

The other notable gaffe this week was turning a day of celebration in Auckland that the long-awaited CRL finally had an opening date into a confused mess about whether National was going to hold a referendum on MMP.

It was an own goal when instead of concentrating on an infrastructure success, or taking a whack at Labour's plan to ditch National's much-loved Investment Boost policy, Luxon loose-lipped his way into an election promise that even his caucus doubted was real.

National would have breathed a deep sigh of relief when the Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll landed on Friday with some good news for the party.

Not only was it up on 31 percent and ahead of Labour, but the coalition was also in a position to form a government and Luxon was up in the preferred prime minister numbers.

Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour has plummeted to 27.8 percent - a dire result that on first glance looks to have come from Luxon ruling out working with Opportunity after the election.

Opportunity has soared to 6 percent in the poll at the expense of Labour.

Labour has been operating on a small-target strategy with policy announcements this election year after learning the lesson of flooding voters in 2023, and losing sight of what the party stood for and was trying to sell.

But the new approach appears to be having its own problems with National getting centrist policy like solar panel loans for households and KiwiSaver policy out ahead of Labour, and leaving the Opposition unable to criticise something it broadly agrees with.

Hipkins also has his own popularity issues to deal with. He's a known quantity having been prime minister before, which he was handed and then had ripped off him when voters went to the polls and chose the other Chris.

He has a difficult job explaining to voters why he'd do a better job second time round.

World.title: Concern Wellington ratepayers will refuse to ration water
World.content:
An advocate for ratepayers says there is a risk Wellington residents will refuse to follow water restrictions, with growing frustration over pricey bills.

Tiaki Wai's first quarterly bills were sent out over the past few weeks, leaving residents shocked at the pricetag, some over $1000.

Come September, Wellington region will be asked to only use sprinklers every second day, and just between the hours of 6-8am and 7-9pm. The Upper Hutt area was already under those restrictions.

James Ross from the Wellington Rates Payers Alliance said the rationing had been unfair for a long time, but had been hidden away in rates bills.

Now, with water charges under a spotlight in a separate Tiaki Wai bill, he said restrictions would likely not be taken well.

"There's a very real concern that people won't be motivated to follow those water restrictions, because frankly I think a lot of people will see them as unfair.

"You've now got these huge water bills ... and yet we're still being told the assests are in such a bad way that you can't use your sprinklers when you need to."

For Ross, this would be solved with water meters, which he said would motivate residents to ration water.

Tiaki Wai planned to roll out water meters so bills reflected actual water use, rather than a fixed rate based on capital value.

However, its draft strategy said installing meters could take between five and seven years, and may cost upwards of $500 million.

Ross said the entity needed to begin this roll out sooner - and cheaper.

He said restrictions were a reality of mismanaged water systems, but meters would allow people to pay for what they actually use.

Tiaki Wai said there was no correlation between water conservation and the amount Wellington property owners have paid for water as part of their rates or will pay as part of their water services bill.

Upper Hutt was always on level one restrictions, following a decision made by the council years ago, a spokeperson said.

Wellington, Porirua and Hutt City were on the restriction during daylight saving months.

The restrictions were to conserve the region's finite water supply, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Wellington, Wairarapa mayors agree to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers
World.content:
Wellington and Wairarapa mayors have agreed to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers by Sunday.

Mayors from the eight councils in the region met this afternoon to discuss plans for a super-merger for local government reforms.

One proposal supported by Wellington, Lower Hutt, Porirua and South Wairarapa District Councils calls for a region-wide merger of all eight councils,

Caterton and Masterton District Councils are proposing a separate Wairarapa-only authority.

Some mayors opposed these ideas but proposals can be submitted against other councils' wishes.

Upper Hutt and Kapiti District Councils have opposed amalgamation.

Kapiti District wanted to submit their own proposal to be a singular unitary authority.

But individual councils cannot submit a proposal to become singular authorities without being part of a larger submission to the ministers.

And other councils disagreed on the grounds that the proposal did not meet the rules of the Head Start programme for local government overhaul.

World.title: Monty Knight's alleged killer's hearing adjourned to determine if she's mentally fit for trial
World.content:
A court hearing for a Northland woman accused of murdering well-known Kaitāia identity Monty Knight has been adjourned so an expert can determine if she is mentally fit to go on trial.

The 57-year-old, who has interim name suppression, was to have had a trial callover hearing in the High Court at Whangārei on Friday.

However, at the request of Crown prosecutor Richard Annandale, the hearing was rescheduled to early December.

He said that was to give psychiatrist Erik Monasterio time to work on a report examining "the issue of insanity".

Annandale said the extra time was needed because Dr Monasterio had much to do.

"The expert is a busy expert and has a large number of matters to attend to," he said.

The judge set a new callover date in December to monitor progress on the report.

Monty Knight was a well-known Kaitāia businessman, wine-maker and local politician. Supplied

A jury trial date had already been set for 5 July next year.

The accused was represented by Sharlene Pilkington, acting for high-profile Whangārei lawyer Arthur Fairley.

Monty Knight died at his home near Kaitāia in November last year. He had recently turned 80.

Ever the entrepreneur, Knight started his retail career with a record shop on the town's main street, then expanded into electronics, appliances and beds.

He took over the family business, Knights the Jewellers, and opened a second outlet in Kerikeri.

When told it was impossible to grow grapes in Kaitāia, Knight proved the doubters wrong by establishing an award-winning winery, Okahu Estate.

He was inducted into the Northland Business Hall of Fame in 2010.

Knight was elected to the Far North District Council in 2010 and the Northland Regional Council in 2015, and ran for the Far North mayoralty a number of times.

He had another tilt at winning a seat on the Far North District Council in the 2025 local elections.

World.title: New jumper revealed as NRL grants Perth Bears salary concessions
World.content:
The NRL's newest side, the Perth Bears, have unveiled their inaugural playing jersey on the same day they were granted salary cap concessions ahead of their entry to the competition in 2027.

In an event coordinated between Perth and North Sydney, where the unveiling was live-streamed, the Bears revealed the jersey by dropping the design from the famous WACA Ground light towers.

The design, which features red hoops on a black background, pays homage the North Sydney Bears, which left the NRL at the end of the 1999 season and currently play in the NSW Cup competition.

Peter V'landys (second from left) announced the concessions alongside WA Premier Roger Cook (speaking), Bears CEO Anthony De Ceglie, and Perth coach Mal Meninga (left). (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

The unveiling of the jersey marks a major step towards the Bears' entry into the NRL, which club chief executive Anthony De Ceglie said was on track to have 35,000 members by the beginning of the 2027 season.

Salary boost

In a big boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys announced the Bears would be granted a concession for signing a marquee player.

"They will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for any player above a million dollars [salary]," V'landys said.

"If the player is worth $1.5 million, they can pay another 20 per cent from a sponsor and that won't be counted in the salary cap.

" So that gives them the opportunity to get somebody because they've got a 20 per cent bonus for that player from the sponsor. "

The Perth Bears will play in the 2027 NRL season. (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

Additionally, the Bears will have first rights to any player who wants to leave their club but is under contract for 2027.

"You may have a marquee player that's not happy in a particular club and the club and the player want to separate. That player can only go to Perth in the first instance," V'landys said.

"There will be some good players that will come up and be given the opportunity to play in Perth."

The concessions will help the Bears land a high-profile player, which has so far being lacking in their signings.

Meninga happy with progress

Bears inaugural coach Mal Meninga says he is "really happy" with the club's progress to date and talked down the need for a marquee player.

"We've worked within the conditions of obviously our entry into the NRL and you know … let me be frank with this … I'm really excited about the roster we've built," he said.

"You look through the team, we've got some high-profile players already.

"We've certainly got players of the future, there's no doubt.

"I really appreciate Peter and the club's great concessions, but I'm really happy with where we are at the moment."

Bellamy excited

Veteran Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy said the arrival of the Bears was exciting for the league.

And he said the club was in good hands with coach Mal Meninga steering the ship.

"I worked with Mal, I played with Mal and I know the amount of work that he puts in and the amount of work he will put into the coaching," he said.

"I'm sure it will be a very successful venture."

The Storm has already seen two of their players, Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, sign on with the Bears, but the coach was magnanimous about their departure.

Tyran Wishart of the Storm will line up for the Bears next season. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

"They're very excited to be coming over here," he said.

"They're obviously doing what they think's best for them and best for their families.

"They're still doing a great job for us.

"That's just the way the game is."

World.title: Live: Warriors dominate in heavyweight clash, Panthers lose captain to injury
World.content:
The New Zealand Warriors have produced one of the best halves of rugby league this season to take a big lead over Penrith, while the Panthers sweat on the fitness of its captain.

The second-placed Sydney Roosters, fresh off scoring 82 points last weekend, host the in-form Canterbury Bulldogs who have surged into the NRL top eight.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.

World.title: De Minaur haunted by Montreal Masters double-fault drama
World.content:
A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Australians through in Montreal Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

AAP

World.title: Ex-AFLPA boss calls for independent tribunal over Cats concussion waiver
World.content:
Former Richmond player and AFL Players Association (AFLPA) chief Joel Bowden has criticised the AFL, Geelong and the AFLPA for their handling of the secret concussion waiver signed by an unknown Cats player, calling for a Senate committee hearing to investigate.

The Cats have avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Speaking to ABC Radio Melbourne on Friday, Bowden said he found it "absolutely outrageous that a young person's been taken advantage of", calling it "gambling with a young [player's] health and safety".

Dogs coach on concussion controversy Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Bowden — who is also a former trade unionist and member of the Northern Territory parliament — pointed to the close ties between the club and the AFL, with former Geelong president Craig Drummond the chairman of the AFL Commission and Geelong chief executive Steven Hocking being the former general manager of football at the AFL.

"How this has got through, how people have thought that this is possibly OK is now ever more outrageous with the facts that have been put on the table," Bowden said.

Loading...

"It's conduct unbecoming. The AFL will fine players, they will fine people who are involved in the community sport — if you breach the code of conduct anywhere in the AFL at a game of community football you can be brought in front of a tribunal.

"And this AFL club, Geelong, have gone and signed a contract outside the standard playing contract and I would say outside of WorkSafe Victoria's legislative framework to provide a duty of care and a safe workplace.

"And now they're going to say: 'Nothing to see here, let's move on and watch the footy.'"

Bowden took aim at his former organisation the AFLPA for putting out a joint statement with the AFL over the issue and saying that the association had to "act more like a union, the union they are."

"They [the AFLPA] are too close [to the AFL] and this example says to me that the industry has got control of the Players Association," Bowden said, citing the AFL's funding of the AFLPA "to the tune of millions of dollars per year".

He called for Geelong to be brought in front of an independent tribunal to get to the bottom of the issue.

"I don't think there's been a press conference where anyone from the AFL or Geelong has stood there and taken questions," he said.

"Concussion is the nmber one issue in the AFL at this point of time. It's going to be huge in years to come, the CTE research and understanding now, the history that we know.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They're all too close and the industry is too close at times so maybe it needs to go to a Senate estimates committee hearing or something and get David Pocock to ask some questions and get independent senators and Sarah Hanson-Young to level these to the AFL.

"A young man has been put at risk and been asked to sign a secret waiver that says he'll exonerate the club from any future issues with his health. That needs to be investigated and that's not OK."

Asked if he thought Geelong would end up being sanctioned over the waiver, he replied:

"Yes I do. I think the court of public opinion will demand that they be sanctioned because this type of behaviour in modern AFL but also in workplace safety laws is not acceptable. Independent separate contracts are unacceptable."

A Victorian government spokesperson responded on Friday.

"Players safety must never be compromised," the spokesperson said.

"The AFL must have evidence-based policies and procedures in place to protect their players.

"The AFL, as the governing body for Australian rules football, has responsibility for managing concussion within the code."

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
World.content:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

World.title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
World.content:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

World.title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
World.content:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.
